utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Puhalic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, the Chamber will deal with the admission of excerpts of prior testimony and statements of Tomislav Kovac used by the Prosecution during his cross-examination. The Chamber does not find it necessary to hear any further submissions from the parties on this issue. The Chamber has reviewed the excerpts proposed by the Prosecution as well as the accused's responses to each as provided to the Chamber's legal staff via e-mail on the 4th of November, 2013, and later amended by the parties on the 7th of November, 2013. Of the 19 excerpts of prior testimony and statements put to Kovac during cross-examination, the Chamber is satisfied that 16 of them were fully read out into the record, and thus the Chamber does not consider it necessary to admit these excerpts into evidence. As agreed upon by the parties, the Chamber considers that the remaining three excerpts were not fully read into the record and therefore would be of assistance to the Chamber. Therefore, the Chamber will admitted following three documents into evidence: 1, 65 ter number 25514, page 39 in B/C/S, and page 52 in English; number 2, 65 ter number 22146, pages 90 to 91 in B/C/S, and pages 383 to 84 in English; and, number 3, 65 ter number 25350, pages 135 to 136 in English. The Chamber instructs the Prosecution to upload the specific pages into e-court for these three documents and instructs the Registry to assign exhibit numbers to them. Shall we give numbers now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 25514 will be Exhibit P6506; 65 ter 22146 will be Exhibit P6507; and 65 ter 25350 will be Exhibit P6508.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want the record to be clear, Mr. President. Because I did review the previous discussions about this in court and it may be seen as a slight modification of the previous practice, but I understand based on explicit discussions with the accused and based on the Court's ruling, that this decision reflects the fact that when the excerpt is read fully into the record and there is no objection by the Defence, then the portion read out in court serves in lieu of the document and as the equivalent of the document. That's been the Defence's position on this matter, and I just wanted there to be no mistake about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We considered that point as well. Shall we continue? Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Puhalic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would just like us briefly to clarify what you meant by some of your answers. Yesterday, on pages 48 and 49, you were asked about killings and beatings. Was this done by some of the staff who administered the beatings? Who killed these people? Were these people killed in the camp? Were they taken away some place? What was the attitude of the staff towards that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about a few of these cases. When people first arrived from the outside, I mean, I cannot remember all the details, but I know that there were a few cases when that's exactly what happened. People were beaten up, and I think that one people -- one person had his or her leg injured. It was late at night or early in the morning when these people would come. I know of these few cases when some of these civilians would say that somebody had been injured, and then I'd go and find a doctor or a nurse or someone to help these people. As for these people, as for the killings, I don't know whether it was two persons that were killed. Major Kuruzovic or someone, I think it was him, I know that he signed this, but I know that later on some person was held responsible for these killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think that it was in the morning when I arrived there, a lady said that her husband was missing for three days already, and then again somebody had come from the outside, and then the major told me to try to find out what happened, so I spent four or five nights right there - how do I put this? - in that house. No, it's not a house. Well, in that house with that Albanian. I spent four or five nights there, and I tried to see who it was that was coming from the outside. But no one was hurt, and then after that that stopped and no one came again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P6051. We don't have to have it called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about that Croatian intercept. Who was it that could have broken in? The document bears the date of the 31st of May. Does this shed more light on what this might have meant, if the date was the 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how should I know? As I've already told you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is misstating the evidence. That intercept actually says to stop a break-out, not people breaking in, but to stop a break-out from the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up the document then for a moment? P6501 actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While I'm waiting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not 6502?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I'm sorry. 6502.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Mr. Puhalic, you were asked -- or, rather, it was confirmed that the conditions were bad. Where did these people live before the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably -- well, at their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Sutherland is right in terms of the interpretation of the Croats, by the Croats, but can you tell us what the situation was on the 31st of May in Prijedor? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, after a few killings by the Muslims, attacks against Prijedor, stopping people going through Kozarac, all these things that happened, so the people who arrived in the camp there, well, there were these extremists, if I can put it that way, who simply took off their uniforms and came to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I'm talking about the broader area of Prijedor. What happened on and around the 31st of May? You mentioned this attack a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attack against Prijedor, and before that, there were a few killings in Prijedor committed by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there any fighting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, if there was an attack against Prijedor, there was fighting. I've already mentioned that. This was armed fighting in Prijedor, all day. And then people probably tried to escape from there and then they arrived in Trnopolje and, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Trnopolje, in your view, was collection centre or reception centre.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 5786. Could that document please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Mr. Puhalic, you confirmed that the infirmary was not particularly well equipped. Where did you resolve matters that could not be resolved at the infirmary in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say. I did not actually deal with that but there was a doctor who was an ethnic Serb, and he probably tried to take people to the hospital in Prijedor, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an assessment of the security situation in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 3 of this document, both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time -- actually, how long were you in Prijedor, until when?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not Trnopolje, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prijedor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any Muslims in Prijedor who had stayed on in town at their homes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please let us focus on the first five lines here. It says that 19.000 households had been registered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic put a question to the witness before reading text from the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was convinced that I had put a question. I was convinced that I had put a question about the Muslims in town who lived in town, and this document precisely says that there were 6.000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember you put that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 3, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He answered yes. And then why do you need this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for him to corroborate that, not only this sentence but others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, please look at the penultimate paragraph. I am going to read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For saving time, I will allow you to continue. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we are going to tender the document, I'm not going to shed any more light on this. I'm going to read out the penultimate paragraph, and then I'm going to put a question to you: "As a consequence of the armed rebellion, reception centres were established at Omarska and Keraterm. Prisoners of war and other persons who had prepared, aided, and organised armed rebellion were placed there, and the homeless and persons who had left their homes of their own free will were housed in the reception centre in Trnopolje." How does this fit into your own knowledge, this bit about Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to all of this, I would agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit the cover page and this page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4010, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I'd just like to ask you this: You discussed the possibility of people returning home with Madam Prosecutor, for these people to return home. Can you tell us in relation to this statement that people could not return home, can you tell us whether that was a decision made by the official authorities? Was that the position of the official authorities? Or was it impossible for them to return home because of something else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they could not return home for another reason, but I don't think that the authorities decided on that. People left their homes, although they could go back home, and as I've already said, with the major's pass, they could return, which was only natural. People did return because they gave up on any further travel, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to draw your attention to the fourth paragraph and I'm going to read out this sentence: "During the fighting and later on, many things happened beyond the official positions that had been taken, property was looted and destroyed, there was abuse, torching, private property was blown up, as well as religious facilities." And then the next paragraph says: "Increased presence of armed personnel led to uncontrolled use of firearms, and the consequence of that are a series of killings, suicides," and so on. Can you tell us how this fits into your own experience? In English it is pages 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases, and that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this page be admitted too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will add that page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, I have no further questions. Thank you, and I do apologise that we had to insist that you come and testify.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Puhalic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter briefly in relation to the two video-clips that were admitted yesterday, one from the Defence and one from the Prosecution. I would just like to let the Chamber know that Mr. Robinson and I are in discussions about the admission of those two exhibits and we will get back to the Court on that in a short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Next witness is Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Kupresanin. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Kupresanin, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that might -- that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you, and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: God help us, President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us remember to make a pause between questions and answers and speak articulately and clearly so we wouldn't have to stop to correct the transcript and waste time. I know you can do that. Have you given a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 1D9198 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not very good at this. I'm trying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see your statement on the screen now? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. I can read it. I'm trying to read. Should I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this that statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I've read a part of the statement. Let me read till the end. I have reached the part where it says, "Community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina." Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No need. Have you read and signed that statement? Did you do it earlier?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the last page so the witness can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you have told my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just leave a short pause before you answer, please. If I were to ask you the same questions today that they had asked you, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I tender this 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection to the admission of this statement, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4011, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the associated exhibits? How many exhibits are you tendering, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Twenty-five, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not 26?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, the fourth document down, 1D09274 has already been admitted, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Any objections, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will deal with item that the Chamber has some problem with. First, 1D9275, referred to in paragraph 50, the Chamber is of the view that that document is not sufficiently commented upon or contextualised to make it inseparable from the witness statement. So if necessary, the accused should lead live about the document. Second, the document referred to in paragraph 42, i.e. 65 ter number 6710, is it not a duplicate of 65 ter 25344, which has been admitted as Exhibit P6437? And the documents referred to in paragraph 35, i.e. 65 ter 9201 and 65 ter 17377, and the final one, 18629, the Chamber would like the accused to lead live as to these three documents. The Chamber is of the view witness needs to provide more context for the documents. And the 65 ter 17367, referred to in paragraph 15, so this seems to be the identical document to 65 ter 17356, referred to in paragraph 8. If the parties could check it. As regards the 65 ter 17516, referred to in paragraph 7, I take it the only three -- first three pages are being tendered. We will admit those three pages. And 17890, referred to in paragraph 44, the -- it has not been sufficiently commented upon by the witness so it -- if the Defence wants to tender that document, Mr. Karadzic should lead live. And para 4, 65 ter 18630, the Chamber does not need it, will not admit it. And 30061, referred to in paragraph 11, which is an intercept, but this seems to be a wrong intercept. This is an intercept between Mr. Karadzic, Krajisnik and Jovan Tintor. But in the statement, witness references a phone conversation between Mr. Karadzic and himself. So if the parties could check it. Finally, 65 ter 1 -- 310 -- I'm sorry, 31700, an intercept referred to in paragraph 14, because the witness does not sufficiently comment upon this document. If the Defence is minded to tender this document, it should lead live. So all the other remaining documents will be admitted into evidence and be given -- assigned numbers in due course by the Registry. Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall now read out in the English language a short summary of the statement of Mr. Vojislav Kupresanin. [In English] Vojislav Kupresanin became engaged in political work on the eve of the first multi-party elections. On March the 4th, 1990, he formed the Yugoslav Democratic Party, the homeland front, and on the 12th of July, 1992, his party became part of the SDS. After this, he was a deputy in the Chamber of citizens in B and H parliament and a member of the SDS Main Board. In the first half of 1992, Mr. Kupresanin was elected president of the assembly of the community of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina and in the second half of the same year, president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, ARK. After the war, he reactivated the work of the homeland front, and on June the 1st, 1993 -- 2003 -- 2013, he retired. The ZOBK was established primarily for economic reasons and included 17 municipalities. After World War II, Banja Luka was economically the second most powerful town first after Sarajevo and the region had several hundred million dollars of commercial surplus, but all this money went to the central bank of Sarajevo. The ZOBK assembly adopted its own statute and had functioned independently of the SDS and any other political party. The ZOBR, there were members of the different parties and everybody worked for the same idea, keeping for the people of Krajina the natural resources of the area. With a basic goal of being able to follow events in the sphere of the economy, politics and culture, the ZOBK assembly took certain liberties from the BH constitution. On June the 28th, 1991, the ZOBK assembly adopted a declaration for the unification of the two Krajinas, RSK and Bosnian Krajina. Dr. Karadzic clearly expressed that he was against this unification and advocated the preservation of existing borders. Dr. Karadzic maintained that these decisions had never been authorised by the SDS Main Board, and although the ZOBK was aware that SDS Main Board decisions were binding for its own members, the local leadership was convinced that all decisions of interest and importance of the two Krajinas were supposed to be made at a level of the Krajinas themselves. The ZOBK assembly had Muslims and Croats who were delegated by municipalities in which they were deputies for the SDA and HDZ until such a time that they stopped coming to the sessions at the instruction of the SDA and HDZ central offices from Sarajevo. Vojo Kupresanin, in his capacity of president of the ZOBK assembly, expressed his wish for the ZOBK to be joined by various Muslim and Croat municipalities because ZOBK goal was not to create a Serbian community. Mr. Kupresanin personally contacted several times Mr. Fikret Abdic, the director of Agrokomerc and a prominent Muslim leader of European orientation, because he wanted this food company to be supplied with the raw material from the area. Unfortunately, Mr. Abdic never replied to these calls. The goal of the ZOBK was to take control of the segments of society which were of significance to Krajina, and in this process, they did not have any co-ordination with the republican organs. In September 1991, the statute of the ARK was adopted. In this statute, all nationalities were recognised as equal and municipalities with a majority of non-Serbian people were enabled to join the ARK. In order to protect the Serbian people in Slavonia, in Croatia, who were exposed to the most heinous crimes, the Serbs in Krajina turned to the JNA for protection. After JNA General Uzelac refused to intervene to defend the Serbs, the ARK decided to declare a mobilisation, which is different from a state of war. Later on, ARK Crisis Staff was established even though the Republika Srpska government ordered the formation of the Crisis Staff per municipalities, not per regions. The reason for the formation of the ARK Crisis Staff was to -- was the tense and alarming situation in BH, and not the expulsion of the non-Serb population from ARK. The ARK Crisis Staff did not receive instructions from the leadership in Pale. Individuals in Krajina respected neither Dr. Karadzic, nor SDS, neither before the war nor in the course of the war. Since neither Dr. Karadzic nor Mr. Kupresanin agreed with the creation of a Krajina state, Mr. Kupresanin managed to prevent the separatist option from being accepted. Meanwhile, Alija Izetbegovic ordered all municipalities to transfer weapons from the police station to Sarajevo ostensibly for a technical inspection, which was interrupted by the Serbs as an intention to leave the Serbian policemen without weapons -- interpreted by the Serbs. For this reason, the regional security centre was established and local Krajina authorities prevented the weapons drain from the police stations. Since in April 1992, Croats and Muslims attacked various Serbian municipalities, the ARK assembly made a decision to form a National Defence council of the ARK and a police department. Dr. Karadzic charged Mr. Kupresanin with responsibility of influencing the leadership in Prijedor to close down investigation centres. Mr. Kupresanin asked the authorities of Omarska and Keraterm to shut down and to improve the prisoners' living conditions until its disbandment. After that, Mr. Kupresanin toured to Manjaca prisoner of war camp, in order to check whether the Geneva Conventions were implemented. Furthermore, Mr. Kupresanin negotiated an end to the fighting in Kotor Varos in agreement with the commander of the VRS operation group and with the chief of the Security Service Centre in Banja Luka. Warring parties and populations surrendered their weapons and the Serbian authorities promised them the creation of conditions for their normal life. The relationship between Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic was always very tense because Mladic placed himself above the assembly and above Supreme Commander. Dr. Karadzic did not have practical control over him. And that's the short summary of the statement of Mr. Kupresanin. At that moment, I do not intend to tender those documents that are to be led live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kupresanin, as you have noted, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is through your written statement, instead of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just before I commence, Mr. President, just one housekeeping matter, perhaps of several that arise from the Court's observations about the exhibits and the statement. So, for example, paragraph 11 is a commentary on a document that we haven't seen, that nobody knows anything about because it's not the document referenced in the paragraph. Barring anything else, I presume that paragraph would then have to come out and that may be true for other sections of the statement in which documents -- well, I think -- certainly wouldn't be the case as far as I can tell for documents that are insufficiently commented on. That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will bear that in mind in reading the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, I understand that although this is the first time you've testified before this Tribunal, that in fact you were interviewed by representatives of the Tribunal, specifically representatives of the Prosecutor's office, on the 16th of July 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And am I correct that it's your position that at that time, you attempted to be as honest and truthful with the -- in giving your answers as you could be?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I tried to tell the truth. Things that I was sure were true, I tried to tell them as I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to your statement before the Court today, the statement that you gave to the Karadzic team. Many of the paragraphs in that statement deal with the two successive regional bodies in the Krajina, the ZOBK and then the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Now, the purpose of the region, that is the region of Krajina, was to eliminate a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct? That is to destroy what was sometimes referred to as Alija's state; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: We turned out at the elections of Bosnia-Herzegovina and automatically we recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina. We chose to live in a democracy and for those three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me -- let me lay out some quick ground rules for you. I'd like you to tend to the question I ask, and I'd like you to only answer the question I asked rather than expound in a manner that you see fit. So in this case, I'm focusing on the task or purpose of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's correct that the purpose of the region, that is the region of Krajina, was to destroy what was sometimes referred to as Alija's state?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: That's not true. The purpose was the economic assertion, self-assertion of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you say that's not true today, but, in fact, that's precisely what you told the members of the Bosnian Serb Assembly at the 20th session held on the 14th and 15th of September, 1992. And we have that in evidence. That's D456. And what you said at English pages 70 and B/C/S page 76 is the following: "Last year, we built up the region and made it strong with the clear purpose and goal, the task of the region of Krajina was to destroy Alija's state." That's what you were saying in 1992, at the time, correct, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I don't remember that. But the region, as time went on, acquired political elements when there were turmoil in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and when the declaration of the Muslim and Croat sides was proclaimed, which practically excluded the Serbian people from the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that context those words could have been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Kupresanin, ensuring that a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina ceased to exist was considered a holy mission, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, I think that Bosnia and Herzegovina should have never been a unitary state, not that it should have been centralised to such an extent that we Serbs were excluded from that state. The ordinary people would never accept such conduct on the part of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, therefore, Mr. Kupresanin, it was your position that ensuring that Bosnia and Herzegovina ceased to exist was a holy mission, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No. That's not it. I probably said that Bosnia-Herzegovina could not exist as a unitary state or a state of Muslims and Croats. Bosnia-Herzegovina must be a state of three constituent peoples. We were equal and we were persistent about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't like to intervene but the follow-up questions of Mr. Tieger are conditioned by the omissions in the transcript. In lines 5 and 6, said that the Serbian people were being excluded as or eliminated as a constituent people, excluded from the republic. Not just as a people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Do you confirm having said that, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember now. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then could you please ask what he said now, not what he said back then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it does not harm the context. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 32152, please. And if we could go to English page 13 and B/C/S page 9 to see who is speaking first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from the extended session held on the 14th of February, 1992, Mr. Kupresanin, a very large plenary, and this is a recording of your comments beginning at page 13 in the English, page 9 of the B/C/S, and concluding at page 15 of the English and page 11 of the B/C/S, where you say: "I personally propose that you suggest to the president of the party and to all our Serbian deputies to make sure that the Serbian police are included in the Serbian constitution. The moment we establish the Serbian police, Bosnia and Herzegovina will cease to exist, and that is our holy mission."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we on correct page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We are still on the first page. I asked to go to page 15 which is the end. I didn't realise we hadn't made that transition. Page 15 of the English, page 13 of the B/C/S -- or page 11 of the B/C/S, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that was your position on the 14th of February, 1992, Mr. Kupresanin, that ensuring that Bosnia and Herzegovina ceased to exist was a holy mission; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: The holy mission was that the Serbian people had to be equal in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There should be no outvoting of the Serbian people. The Serbian people had to be a constituent people with all the elements and rights which any other people in Europe has in any other democratic country. Because the Serbian people was having less and less of that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then we began to form our political positions. One of them was to constitute the assembly of Republika Srpska, and then the government, the constitution, and everything else followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kupresanin. Please try to answer the question. You answered it and then you started to tell us what followed. I'm asking you not to make dissertations, just to focus on the question. In fact, Mr. Kupresanin, you stated, to applause at that session, that the goal was to finally live in one country and not have Serb territories divided. And that's found on the previous page of both documents, both the English and B/C/S documents.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question? Because I haven't understood. What did I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, you said at 1992 that the holy mission was destroying Bosnia-Herzegovina and the goal was for the Serbian people to finally live in one country; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, any conscious people or an individual within a people has a tendency for the people to live in one country. Germany caused two world wars, and in spite of 100 million victims, in 1998, the Germans were allowed -- or rather in 1989, the Germans were allowed to live in one country. And in both world wars we were on the side of the allies. We are the only people in Europe who is forbidden to live in one state. So what is bad about that? I'm thinking to this day, and I tend and wish for my people to live in one Serbian country, and that is my democratic right. Any tendency of an individual to such a goal is the holy mission of any individual, and this is something I'm not going to deny. I still want the Serbian people to have one single Serbian state in the Balkans, and I think that we deserve this because we participated on the side of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender the document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in this case could we receive the whole document? He speaks again at the end, and I think it's better to have the whole document in for context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit these pages and, if necessary, deal with those pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P6509.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kupresanin, you were aware that the Bosnian Serb leadership, the republic level and particularly Mr. Karadzic, backed and were behind regionalisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: In case of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Radovan Karadzic was not to be found even in traces. Whatever happened about the region had to do with the MPs who were from the region and municipal deputies. I'm not aware of Radovan Karadzic having participated in any way. I know that the constitutive session was held in Celinac. There were several people who were candidates. It never occurred to me that I might be the president. Because after a heart attack I had come from a hospital, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will get to all that information in a second. In fact, Mr. Kupresanin, Mr. Karadzic bragged to you about his role in regionalisation, didn't he, in telephone conversations with you both before and after the establishment of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I don't remember such bragging. I don't think it happened. I don't remember that at all. Before Krajina, we never discussed this issue. After its establishment, I doubt that we did. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you read the documents which are associated with your statement; for example, D1084 cited in paragraph 30, or D424 cited in paragraph 29? Or were those just appended to the statement by someone else?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I didn't read them. I don't read them here now. I don't know whether I read them or not. You asked me a specific question and I gave you a specific answer. Now, I don't know whether you expect something further from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at those two documents which are specifically referenced in your statement. First of all, D1084, which is an intercept, intercepted telephone conversation, between you and Dr. Karadzic on the 23rd of July, 1991. The transcript says D. It's P1084. Now, just to refresh your memory about that, there is a discussion about the possible -- somebody raising the possibility of a referendum about Krajina to which Dr. Karadzic responds, Are they fucking nuts? And you say, So, what do you suggest for us to do? And the conversation continues. Dr. Karadzic tells you why that wouldn't be a good idea, including the fact that it would be a mistake for negotiations because they have even prepared complete documentation to show John Major?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we on correct page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. That would be page 3 of P1084, in the English, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIGER
utterances.text: And B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They prepared documentation with all the evidence that the Serbs are creating the Greater Serbia. And now you are playing right into their hands as if they are paying you. Fuck, man. And then he continues at the bottom of that page, and then continues on to the next page, These are some fools who show up making premature steps. That will happen, Vojo, but they have to be - "they" meaning the Muslims - have to be responsible for that. They have to make a mistake. They will definitely make a mistake. We know that. And so you ask, Shall I call you tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters into B/C/S did not find the relevant passage and could not quote the original words of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, it's on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that speed interpreters cannot [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. That's page 4 of the B/C/S. They have to make a mistake. They will definitely make a mistake. We know that. And then Dr. Karadzic continues in the middle of the page in English and a little further on in B/C/S, What the fuck else am I supposed to do? Who created that fucking regionalisation? Then he goes on at the bottom of the page in English to talk about how he views the appropriate way to be a certain winner by not keeping your plans on your forehead and playing into other people's hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, that's what he told you in July of 1991, Mr. Kupresanin. Why don't we look at what he said to you in February of 1992, after the formation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and that's D424, also explicitly referenced in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it seems like the witness ought to be given a chance to answer some question, otherwise Mr. Tieger is just making some kind of closing argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I am responding to the witness's -- I'm presenting the witness with evidence in response to his assertion that he never discussed regionalisation with the accused before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness read the document and then why don't you ask a question. Do you follow the intercept? Did you read the parts read out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying, but it doesn't really seem to work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Should witness be given the hard copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any difficulty with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What am I supposed to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't care what you read, Mr. Kupresanin. I recited to you some of the pertinent portions of this document and certainly sufficient portions to ask you the question: Isn't it true that it is -- let me put it this way: It is incorrect, it is not true, that you did not discuss regionalisation with Dr. Karadzic, as you just testified to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I don't remember that Radovan Karadzic and I discussed the issue of the regionalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina at any given time. I just know that all of Europe is divided into regions. It has 10.000 regions. We wanted to be like Europe. We wanted to copy Europe. And all the time we were saying Yugoslavia should join the Europe. Europe is being regionalised. We wanted to copy that, so where is the sin there? If we had regions it wouldn't mean that we wanted to topple Bosnia-Herzegovina. They would strengthen it economically in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's stick on the topic. I'm not asking for your justifications of regionalisation. I'm asking you about this: So now that you say you don't remember that you and Dr. Karadzic discussed regionalisation at any given time, can you explain to me how it is that your statement explicitly references this conversation and incorporates it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's do it in this way. Mr. Kupresanin, do you have your statement with you now? Your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 23rd of July, 1991, how come that it's the 23rd of July when Krajina was formed on the 24th of June? It's possible that this conversation took place after the constitution of the assembly of the autonomous region, because it was on the 24th of April, 1991, that we constituted the assembly of Krajina. So the region came into being at certain point, and this conversation was conducted after it came into being and not before that, as far as I can notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, do you remember that telephone conversation with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I don't remember at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have your statement with you now, witness statement that Mr. Karadzic tendered? We will print out for you. We can upload his statement. Paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If I may, Excellency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you see the paragraph 13 of your statement? I will read out for you, "I have been shown document" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it, I can see it, I can see it, I can see it, and I'm reading it now. Please don't help me. I'm going to do it by myself. I understand this perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The telephone conversation referred to in this paragraph 13, i.e. P1084, is what you have now with you now. Just a minute ago you said to us you don't remember that telephone conversation. So how can you comment on this telephone conversation while you do not remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the telephone conversation did take place, but I cannot confirm that 100 per cent. I remember the topic of this conversation. I know what it was about, and I know that Mr. Karadzic, when it comes to this unification of the autonomous regions of Krajina, Radovan Karadzic did not participate in this process in any way whatsoever. It was the result of work of the MPs from the Autonomous Regions of Krajina. Actually, he did not want to approve of this activity of ours, saying that we simply had to apply in practice the positions of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party, and sometimes we did something that was not in accordance with it, not all of us, but as far as I can see from this document, the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I give an explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You can deal with it in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It concerns an inaccuracy of the question. It's a big confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not hearing any objection to the questions when they are asked and the witness has answered, and to traverse back to the colloquy seems to be counter-productive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please discuss it or deal with it in your re-examination, Mr. Karadzic. In the meantime, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when it came time for the Autonomous Region of Krajina to be established in September of 1991, you mentioned that establishment in paragraph 16 of your statement, it happened that despite initiatives to do that earlier, those hadn't passed, and then all of a sudden it happened that it was allowed to establish. It was allowed to establish such a region, right, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina allowed us to constitute the region. Article 4 of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina allowed for the regionalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina on various bases, the economic basis, the closeness of territories, and so on. The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina allowed us to do that. So there was no legal vacuum in that respect. We were not doing anything wrong. We were doing this in accordance with the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't quite the question. Let me try it this way, Mr. Kupresanin. This Trial Chamber has received that on the 6th of September, Dr. Karadzic said to Slobodan Milosevic that the next day he was having a big plenary "with all my officials." And that's P2544. And the next day, as we know from P2530, the Pale symposium of municipal, regional and republic SDS organs was held, and that resulted in decisions and conclusions about regional organisation. And at that meeting, as we know from the words of a Main Board member or in the words of a Main Board member, which is reflected in P2545, "We passed a decision yesterday...," and this was a conversation this Main Board member was having on September 8, so he's referring back to September 7: "We passed a decision yesterday that Bosnia can remain officially but we'll split it into Serbian Bosnia, Croat Bosnia and Muslim Bosnia." So those were the steps taken by the republic level authorities to advance regionalisation, correct, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I don't remember that at all. I just know that the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina allows for regionalisation, that it was no sin and it was no conflict with the law or the constitution, that people were allowed to join a region and establish it. And as for Radovan Karadzic, Slobodan Milosevic, instructions, I don't remember that at all, or that it happened, or that it was some kind of strategy, really, political or otherwise. But according to the law, it was possible to establish regions and why would we hold it against people if they wanted it and could do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And from your point of view, back in 2001, reflecting back on what happened in 1991 and 1992, all of a sudden it happened that it was allowed for the Krajina officials to establish the region; right? And you said that in your interview, which is 65 ter 25608, at page 15 of the English and page 20 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I don't have page 20 here. I don't see it. There is page 17 and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 25608, page 15 of the English, page 20 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's line 20 through 22 for your benefit, sir. And lines 36 through 37 in the English. That's what you explained some 12 years ago when these events were fresh in your mind; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: This is so vaguely written that I can't understand it. Nothing is really said here. What was possible, what was not, what people were allowed to, it was well known what people could do and what was allowed, what we could do and what was allowed we did that. We did not threaten Bosnia-Herzegovina. We did not violate the constitution. So I don't see what was bad about this and this is very sloppily written.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It may be sloppily written but it reflects your verbatim words at the time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that portion, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you read out from line 20 to 22, your answer. Could you read out aloud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "There were earlier initiatives to organise a region in this area, but it was not upheld. And suddenly it so happened that it was allowed to establish a region. Probably we need the critical mass for such a project like that and probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will admit this page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6510, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, you assert in your statement at paragraphs 29, 33, 34, that one of the issues that you claim reflected the insubordination or independence of autonomous region of Krajina figures was the push for unification with the Krajina, with the Croatian Krajina, Knin Krajina, and you state that you were the one who prevented that. And again that's found at paragraphs -- the latter assertion is found at paragraphs 33 and 34.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No. I advocated the unification of the two Krajinas. I did. And the other side, the Serbian Democratic Party and Radovan Karadzic, didn't. We announced the declaration on the 28th of June, 1991, which said the Republic of Serbian Krajina will join the remaining part of Yugoslavia. So, for the Serbs, it was somewhat acceptable that the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro and Serbia should be in one state, a smaller state, where Serbs and Muslims would live together as the two dominant ethnic groups. That was our political platform, our political will, and this Grahovo declaration never really took off the ground. And what happened happened. Serbs have been expelled from Croatia and it turns out that that was better than --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's focus on the questions at hand. So do you -- do I understand then that you recant the statement that you endorsed no more than a half hour ago, I think, at paragraphs 33 and 34 where you say you -- I managed to prevent the separatist option. That's 33 and paragraph 34 at the session. I managed to prevent the option of the Krajina separatists from being accepted. Because in your statement you take credit for preventing the option that you now say you advocated.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, I did not sign this decision. I didn't sign it because the majority, mostly from the Serbian Democratic Party, were against it, including President Karadzic himself, because they were saying the time was not yet ripe for this. And time passed, we never did it, precisely at the initiative of the President of Republika Srpska and the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. It was our great wish to unite with the Serbs from the Republic of Serbian Krajina. They remained a minority. They were victims of genocide in the Second World War and they ought to have been protected at any cost. I don't think that Radovan Karadzic was the crucial man who dismantled the project. I think that Slobodan Milosevic in Serbia actually prevented the Republic of Serbian Krajina from joining the rest of Yugoslavia, and that is a big sin that the majority of the Serbian people committed towards the Serbs from the Republic of Serbian Krajina, because that minority of the Serbian people are the remains of the Serbian people whose throats had been cut in Croatia. A million and 900.000 Serbs lived in Croatia before the Second World War and the Second World War ended in Croatia with 700.000 Serbs left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please, I -- I would ask you, it's not pleasant to have to interrupt you, and I don't wish to do so, but I hope you can see that you're straying quite far from the precise subject at hand. Now, what you just said, and I'll -- that the -- the initiative didn't happen because of the intervention of the President of Republika Srpska, because of Dr. Karadzic's opposition, is precisely reflected in what happened at the 8th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 25th of February, 1992, where you spoke at the assembly and said that you couldn't handle the situation. Just let me get your exact words, sir: I can't bear the entire burden of that Krajina assembly on my shoulders. And you urged that the president of the party and the president of the assembly come to Banja Luka to make sure that nothing bad happens, and you explained to the Members of Parliament, "I know...," and this is a quote: "I know that Karadzic, as the president of the SDS, is truly the leading figure among the Serbian people and five of his sentences are enough to change the entire course of the session." So contrary to your statement where you take -- you take credit for preventing the Krajina option from being realised. At the time you said you couldn't do it, only Radovan Karadzic could do it, and in fact he came to Banja Luka on the 29th of February and he prevented that from happening. That's what happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No. You've confused your topics and all these theses. It's not the uniting of the two Krajinas. In Bosnian Krajina there was this project by a number of intellectuals to create Republika Srpska. In the area of Banja Luka, and Krajina and these 17 municipalities, a number of intellectuals advocated that project and they were persistent in that. I asked the President of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, to come to Banja Luka so that we could do something about that. I myself could not do anything about it. I couldn't prevent it, I couldn't dispute it, and so on and so forth. So you confused these topics. It's not that it's the integration of a state. This is within one region. There was this idea to create a republic from Grahovo to Derventa. And the Serb people would not be in an entity. There would not be a territorial link. The Serb people should not be forgotten in the Krajina. Sir, I think that you have confused these topics, and you don't seem to know of this other case -- you don't seem to be very knowledgeable on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, in paragraph 33, you say: I managed to prevent this separatist option. And that refers to -- that refers to P938, which is a discussion that took place on the 28th of February, 1992, and it's about the declaration of the Republic of the Krajina; correct? And at paragraph 34 you say that there was a session of the ARK assembly the next day and you managed to prevent the option of the Krajina separatists from being accepted. And that's all part of your thesis that Dr. Karadzic wasn't involved in this whole effort; right? So you're taking credit for preventing the declaration of the Republic of Krajina. That's what you say in your statement. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: You said a moment ago, during the establishment of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina that Radovan Karadzic took part in this project. I said that Radovan Karadzic did not take part in this project of the creation of the autonomous region in any way. Now we are moving on to another problem, and that is the creation of a state within a state, a state within a state. We already have Republika Srpska, and we have an attempt within Republika Srpska to create yet another state which is going to be called the Krajina within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we have a state within a state. That is a different situation. And of course I asked Radovan Karadzic for his help. I asked him to help me so that we would prevent the creation of a state within a state. That is that case. And it has nothing to do with what you've been saying all along. And you don't seem to be understanding what I have been saying and that is the truth. And Radovan Karadzic came --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did not manage to prevent the separatist option. You didn't prevent the option, as you say in both those paragraphs. It was Dr. Karadzic, the man whose five sentences can change the course of an entire assembly -- session as you said at the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 25th of February, 1992. And you're taking credit for that instead of giving it to him because you want to remove him from any contact with the operation of the Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I've been talking about the state of Krajina here, within Bosnia-Herzegovina that was supposed to be constituted. I wanted to have that prevented. Not to split up the Serb people, not to create yet another state. And that's why I called President Karadzic to help us. He came and he persuaded people that this was nonsense, that this was stupid, and that we should give up on that project. And I think that he did well. Quite simply, Radovan's five sentences meant more than who knows how many speeches of mine. So there seems to be this confusion of topics here and I kindly ask you to focus on this creation of the Krajina. This is in Bosnia. It has nothing to do with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Time for a break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kupresanin, we will have a break for 30 minutes and resume at 10 past 11.00, but there is one thing I'd like to deal with in your absence. Could you excuse yourself first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will resume at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, I want to ask you next about Mr. Brdjanin, the president of the ARK Crisis Staff. Now, this Trial Chamber has received evidence that, for example, at the anniversary session of the founding of the SDS, which was held on the 12th of July, 1991, that's P6243, Mr. Brdjanin said, I am a man who abides by two principles. I obey and respect those who are above me, all those who are under my command must obey me. And he went on to explain that's why he supported the central Sarajevo leadership. Now, that's in part also how you perceived and understood Mr. Brdjanin, as a man who, among other things, tried to be as close as possible to the leadership, to those above him; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, you said that Brdjanin was president of the Crisis Staff. I don't know on whose instructions the Crisis Staff was formed in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The Crisis Staff in the Autonomous Region of the Krajina was not initiated by the assembly of the autonomous region and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. We may well get into that subject but I thought my question was reasonably clear. It was about Mr. Brdjanin and not about the establishment of the Crisis Staff of which he was the president.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, if possible, to repeat that as succinctly as you put it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me try it a slightly different way. You understood Mr. Brdjanin, based on your contacts with him, as somebody who tried to be close to people -- the people above him, who wanted to push himself forward in politics by doing so, who liked people in high positions, and whose world was basically the people who were on the top; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, how should I know? He was devoted to this idea that the Serb people should live in freedom. Now, to what extent he was a person who liked power, I really don't know. When he and I worked in the Krajina, he was my vice-president, although at the time he was also a minister. We had little contact. What he stated is his view of the world. That is what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in 2001, when these events were presumably fresher in your memory, you also indicated that you didn't have extensive and regular contact with him but you said that was because he was a guy whose world was the people on the top. He was -- he liked and was into the people in high positions. And that's your explanation for the limitations on your contact with him; right? The fact that he was devoted to the people on the top.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so. These people were not the classical top, as you would put it. We are not the same, all of us. We have different affinities. I am basically interested in my people. It's not that I strove to be someone in some position. I stood in the defence of my homeland and I sought my own happiness in the happiness of my own people, and I sought my own wealth in the wealth of my own people. Brdjanin perhaps had ambitions that were greater than my own, in terms of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript, although witness repeated it but it should be in the second line, about ambition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I understand it, what the witness said that's reflected in the last line is apparently something that he said a bit earlier in the answer. Is that it? It's apparently contained in the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you then to confirm what you said in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, if we could turn it's 65 ter 25608, and if we could turn first to English page 15 and B/C/S page 20, lines 28 through 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page in English, and as I said, on page 20 in the B/C/S, you're explaining the difference between you and Brdjanin painting yourself as someone who prefers to be independent and retain self initiative in contrast to those: "Who want, who are pushing themselves in politics. They want to be bigger than they are. And in order to achieve that, you know, one has to be a poltroon, you know, sort of stuck up too high or people in higher levels."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I think that -- I mean, it's not that I think that Mr. Karadzic liked people who were sort of people who wanted to be lizards, sycophants at all costs. I admired people for their work, their ideas, their efforts. I took care of the people. That was my holy mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay at page --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: And Brdjanin --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pardon me, could the witness please be shown the top of the next page so that he would have full insight?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also said at page 28 of the English, lines 8 through 11, and page 39 of the B/C/S - if we could turn to those - lines 14 through 18, that Brdjanin: "Liked people who were in high positions, and I wasn't like that. We didn't communicate at all, not even on the phone." So that's another --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I did not telephone or I did not communicate with who?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is what you're saying about Brdjanin in 2001; correct? This is a taped interview, Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I did not understand you. Are you saying that I did not communicate with Radovan Karadzic and the political leadership or that did I not communicate with Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm reading to you verbatim from the answers you gave to the representatives of the Prosecutor on July 16th, 2001, about Mr. Brdjanin and you said he liked people who were in high positions and you weren't like that. That's correct? That's what you said at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, it's correct that I did not communicate often. That is correct, that I did not communicate often. Probably there was no need to, although he was president of the Crisis Staff, because I have my own position regarding the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, at page 68 of the English, line 41, and page 100 of the B/C/S, line 33, again referring to Mr. Brdjanin, you said: "He had his own world, his people were the top, on the top."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: That was probably the rule for him. He had his own ideals, his own idols. I had my own. I'm not trying to say that people who were top leaders were not persons of authority for me, but I thought that I was supposed to work hard, work honourably, work honestly in order to get a position and to be held in their regard, that I should have certain merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender those excerpts, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just the basis to -- of tendering them? He confirmed his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we indicated, he confirmed portions of those and portions were sort of edged around. I think with the clarity being dramatically enhanced if we simply have exactly what he said in 2001, and I mean those are classical documents for admission, I think they would be helpful and render the record more clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is primarily a matter for the Chamber. But it implicates the very same issue that we had in the Kovac, if you feel that the portion has been fully read then it's not necessary to admit it, but if you feel there is something that's ambiguous about what was read and what the answer was, then it can be assistance to the Chamber and it can be admitted. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And one more point on that, Mr. President, if I may, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the general position as to the prior consistent statement of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, a prior consistent statement is not admissible unless it's to rebut an allegation of recent fabrication, but a prior inconsistent statement is admissible either by his oral -- orally indicating that that's what he said or by the record of what he said being read to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry to intervene too quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll come back to you unless it is related to this debate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I just only would like to point out that what Mr. Robinson said was allocated to your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those things do get fixed. A couple of things, Mr. President. Number one, the prior consistent statement rule is a rule that arises out of a classical adversarial system for reasons related to the hearsay rule, which have no application here. The question is the relevance and utility of any statement, not whether or not if facially offends the rule against hearsay and then thus requires a separate exception for its admission. So citation to that particular rule arising from the jurisdiction that Mr. Robinson and I both hail from, I think, is not applicable here. Number two, the -- I revert back to my earlier point, the -- I -- the Kovac decision presumably arises as an exception. We dealt with those issues before. This -- in a very similar situation, repeatedly and I can cite the Court to that. It's T42198. The same issue arose. The point was made by the Prosecution counsel that it's better and clearer to actually have the document in, and the Trial Chamber agreed, better to have them in written evidence. And I would say that that is the case for a couple of reasons, because we have -- there are many occasions in which we present to witnesses for impeachment purposes and recite portions of evidence which we don't consider to be admissible - Court knows that - written statements which fall within 92 bis. So now we're -- rather than admitting the document and therefore having it clear, we now will have two categories of questions, one of which is to be used in lieu of the underlying document, others of which are not admissible and are only questions. And unless we make that clear during the time the question is posed, which is not likely to happen and hasn't been happening, we introduce a potential ambiguity into the record. Far clearer, it seems to me, to simply make the decision at the time. Of course this is admissible. It either clarifies, contextualises, or impeaches what the witness says, is of valuable to the Court for that reason, and we have it in evidence and can refer to it, rather than reading the context in which the question is raised to decide it's not one of those questions for which evidential value is or is not to be attributed, but is, instead, one of those that refers to a document that wasn't admissible. In the Kovac case, in this case, we are obviously dealing with documents that are admissible, prior statements. I think the Kovac ruling was based on the clarity of that particular record and perhaps the number of examples. But as a general rule, this Court has already taken the position that it's -- it's better and clearer to have them in written evidence. And I continue to think that we'll have a clearer record and one much easier to work with if we do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm not sure the Chamber necessarily agrees with your observation that the prior consistent statement rule is not applicable at all. There are two matters with respect to this interview, part of this interview. First, whether this is a -- this part is inconsistent with this witness's evidence; and number two, whether the -- there is a need to admit this part separately. The Chamber will put this under advisement, to make a more informed decision and we will come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I appreciate that, Mr. President. That's fine. Let me simply say I tried to get into it in a -- what I consider to be a fair way. I asked the witness the question first. We didn't get the direct answer, instead moved away, so I said, Well, fine then, didn't you say this, and we still didn't get quite the adoption that I think would be -- that would completely reflect the statements that were made. Okay. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you next, Mr. Kupresanin, about other aspects of Mr. Brdjanin. Now, you considered that he was responsible for things for which he should be prosecuted; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Concerning Mr. Brdjanin I can say that he didn't do anything in practical terms that would harm other people and other nations. Mr. Brdjanin was wont to say things occasionally, but his words are one thing and his acts were something different. There were verbal excesses, things he said that I didn't agree with, but in practical life I never noticed that he harboured any hatred towards other ethnic communities. He even had a lot of friends and socialised a lot with Muslims from Celinac, from other places. I don't think -- I didn't see that he had any antagonism or hatred towards other ethnic communities.
