And he -- in his discussions in the assembly, I never heard him say anything ugly. That's how I see Mr. Brdjanin, except that sometimes he would say something that was over the top. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think you're sufficiently clear about the position you're taking now here in this Court in 2013, so I want to look at what you said in 2001. First of all, back -- still on 65 ter 25608, at page 68 of the English, page 99 of the B/C/S, English page -- lines 1 through 8 on page 68, and lines 26 through 30 of the B/C/S, you said, "What I put on his soul" -- excuse me. First of all, you said you consider him responsible for things for which "he should be prosecuted." See at the top: "And for those things he should be prosecuted. I think Radoslav Brdjanin is responsible for certain things. What are those things? And for things he should be prosecuted." And then you went on to say: "What I put on his soul are statements in -- to which the other people of other nationalities -- nationalities had great problems and probably those statements made them move partly." So you said those two things; right? The B/C/S goes on to the next page, lines 3 to 8.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I never said this. I never said this. I have the impression that something is being foisted on me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a transcript of a tape, Mr. Kupresanin. At page -- again at page 68 of the English, again page 100 of the B/C/S, lines 21 through 22 of the B/C/S, you said: "I think that his statements contributed to the great danger that -- that Croats and Muslims were put into and probably one part of them moved out because of those things." You said that as well about Mr. Brdjanin in 2001.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I don't think I've said this. I said a moment ago what I said, that he was wont to make verbal excesses, to say things that were over the top. So maybe -- maybe there were some problems because of that. I still stand behind my belief that whatever -- whoever did anything against other peoples should be held responsible. If somebody incited expulsions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, could you repeat your answer? And speak very slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember this. I said what I've said, and what I've noticed about Brdjanin. It's possible that I said this but I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You heard from Muslims -- excuse me, you heard from Serbs that Brdjanin had said that only a thousand Muslims would remain in Banja Luka, and that's found at page 43 of the English and page 64 of the B/C/S. These are at lines 15 through 18 in the B/C/S. That's correct also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No, no. I never heard Brdjanin say that just a thousand Muslims would live in Banja Luka, only a thousand. A normal person would never say that. I've never heard him say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But that's what you said in 2001.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I never said that Brdjanin had said that only -- it's not true, Mr. Prosecutor, that I said that he had said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Kupresanin, you said -- as I said before, you said in 2001 that Serbs told you that Brdjanin said that -- and that's what you heard from Serbs, that only a thousand Muslims would remain in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Sir, it is such nonsense. I've never said that. It would never occur to me. Nobody told me anything of the kind, nor did I hear Brdjanin ever say that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown that precise line so that he can read for himself what he had stated at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or you could read out the entire context. I'm not sure that we have a correct page on B/C/S. I will read out the portion. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think so. I think we have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under which number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Have you heard him on TV saying that only a thousand Muslims would stay in Banja Luka? "I didn't hear that myself but I heard that he had said that."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's all right. That's all right. No, no. I heard, when Brdjanin addressed a number of journalists from the BH television in response to their question how many Muslims should come back, and he then mentioned a percentage. I don't remember which percentage, but it sounded odd to me and it was an unpleasant surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also heard from Muslims that they were afraid of him; correct? And you said that in 2001 at page 64 of the Serbian, lines 6 through 8, and page 43 of the English, line 39.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I heard that Brdjanin said at some point that he mentioned cabbage, saying that cabbage should not be pickled. That's what Muslims told me about what he said on that subject, that they should not expect to eat pickled cabbage, and that's what I heard from the Sarajevo journalists, and this other thing regarding the pickling of cabbage. I took this out of context - maybe he said something in greater detail - and what people told me later, that it's no use pickling cabbage because there would be no time to eat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. Line 20, there is something missing. The witness said: The Muslims told me that. I did not hear it from Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic -- Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you also stated that Brdjanin was someone who wanted to impose radical nationalist solutions for the benefit of one national group against the rights of other national groups; is that correct? And I can turn you to the passage that reflects that, if you like.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I would like to see it. I don't remember saying something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 56, English, please, and page 82, B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked, Would you say that the persons who were the most -- whether Brdjanin was among persons who were the most radical in Krajina at the time. You said, I don't know what the term radical means, sometimes the term radical it's negative, sometimes it represents fascism, et cetera, sometimes it's positive. Then it was explained -- then you asked, You elaborate. What do you mean by radical? And the -- your interlocutor stated, When I say radical, I mean radical nationalist, someone who wants to impose solutions, radical nationalist solutions for the benefit of one national group against the rights of other national groups. And your answer was, I understood. Well, judging by his appearances and/or his attitude, what he said, Brdjanin had all those elements and more than that. That was your position in 2001, correct, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, all right. Brdjanin had a national bias. Whether he was nationally aware, I don't know. I did not see any extremism or chauvinism in his public appearances. It was more verbal on his part, a populist rather than putting it into practice on the ground. He was more into public appearances when he said such things in the assembly. He did not speak like that. I don't believe he was in the -- on the board. I know he socialised with Muslims. He had very close friends among Muslims. His entire family and his wife, they even participated in some --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what they participated in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I don't think he hated other ethnicities. But if he thought that would give him a political advantage, then on such occasions that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd tender those excerpts, too, Mr. President. And just to be clear, I'm certainly not urging that where there is a clear-cut, straightforward and unequivocal adoption of a prior statement, that that needs to be admitted in -- in -- in that sense, and we've acknowledged that before. So if that's what Mr. Robinson meant by previous prior consistent statement, I -- I don't want to argue that we need to have those admitted. We have take that position clearly before. But in these cases I think we continue to have ambiguity and the record is rendered much clearer by the admission of these excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What are those pages you refer to? What pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page -- at the English, page 68. Page 64 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think 64 was shown to the witness at all. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And page 56 of the English and 82 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sixty-eight, 56, and 64. I would like you to deal with -- whenever you -- immediately after you dealt with the document, I'd like to deal with their admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Each -- each -- each separate is okay, even if it's the same topic. We'll do, Mr. President. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will deal with it all together later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you -- you mentioned in your previous answer something about thinking about gaining political advantage. And, in fact, you stated in 2001, that he probably served a purpose to someone in -- with these extreme positions; correct? So we turn to page 43 of the English and page 63 of the B/C/S. And in 63, lines 30 through 31, you said he was forcing himself to be the leader of the Serbs in the Krajina region and he probably served his purpose to someone as being an extreme person, correct, that's what you said in 2001?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I see that I've said that and I probably did, but I'll be more precise now. I believe Mr. Brdjanin was in communication with the army on this subject. That's my opinion. And I believe that he did not communicate on that subject at all with Mr. Karadzic. He adored officers and generals. I was sometimes in conflict with them but his relationship with them was ideal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to something else you said, and that's at page 68 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, okay, I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I will -- I will add that page to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also said the following, if you turn to transcript page 68 in the English and 102 through -- 102 in the B/C/S, moving on to 103 as we continue towards the bottom of the B/C/S at page 102. So starting at line 40 you said, We didn't socialise. He had his own world -- again, we are speaking about Mr. Brdjanin. He had his own world. His people were the top, on the top. Let me just say something. All his speeches and all those statements and actions could have been cut off by somebody and somebody could have shortened his horns. I wonder why people who were able to do that didn't do it, because such statements and such accents -- actions of his only damaged or created damage for the Serb people. So the president of the country could have done it, the president of the assembly could have, parliament -- I'm sorry, the parliament -- president of the parliament, president of the government, or the prime minister. Why did they tolerate it? Maybe they agreed with him, I don't know. That's what you said in 2001, correct, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: What I know regarding Radovan [as interpreted] Brdjanin and the president of Republika Srpska is this: I believe they were in constant conflict over Brdjanin's behaviour. If Brdjanin thought that something he had done was good, then the president would tell him in so many words that it was idiotic, that he had shot himself in the foot with such behaviour, and it very often happened that Radovan criticised him every now and then saying, Why did you do this and why did you do that? He simply sought explanations from some of his actions. That's what I know from some people who were there. Now, what you are saying, perhaps Radovan could have or Momo could have, I don't think he was close in any way with either Momo or Radovan. Maybe he had some ambitions of becoming a minister, but he often made serious slips, blunders, and Radovan could not understand his actions, he just couldn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not what I'm saying, Mr. Kupresanin, it's what you said in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this excerpt as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the statements Mr. Brdjanin made that you said in 2001 provoked fear among the Muslims and caused a portion of them to leave were not the only statements by Krajina leaders reflecting issues about the number of Muslims who remained in the ARK region. For example, Mr. Kupresanin, you were also concerned about the number of Muslims in the territory comprised or anticipated to comprise Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, I was concerned about Muslims and Croats because of the situation they found themselves in. They found themselves in a very difficult situation because they had the obligation to serve in our army under the law and wage war against their own, and they tried in every possible way to avoid that obligation, and in that I understood them. Second, we didn't have factories during the war. In fact, we had factories but they were not operating and people were very hard up. I talked several times with the president of the republic, saying that conditions should be created to enable them to make a living. Serbs mainly came from villages into towns, but they still had their home farms from which they could draw sustenance; whereas Muslims were mostly urban population, and workplaces and factories were for them the only source of livelihood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's an adequate answer for this purpose. Your position that the only expression or the only time you gave expression to concerns about the number of Muslims in Republika Srpska was for their benefit is contradicted by any number of things that you said in 1992 through 1995. For example, at the third session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, D84, at English pages 26 through 27 and B/C/S 41 through 42, you told the assembly members that in your view, our, that is Bosnian Serb living space, and the territory in which they live was endangered, and that danger has to be averted, and then you talked about shutting off the 250- to 300.000 Muslims in Cazin Krajina into a ring. That was one expression of your concern about the number of Muslims who might be in territories sought by or intended to comprise Republika Srpska, wasn't it, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I don't know that Muslims from the Cazin Krajina made up or were comprised in Republika Srpska. They were a separate region. I don't remember who their main boss was. And before the war, I had a lot of communication with them about integration and co-operation. During the war, we had great problems with the Cazin Krajina. We had to keep a lot of personnel occupied to defend ourselves from them. But I was talking about the autonomous region of Republika Srpska, not the Cazin Krajina. At that time we were at war. Why would I be thinking about them? And of course, we had to narrow down the front line during the war. We were in jeopardy, physically, and in economically, and it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, I asked you about something that you said before the war, at the third session of the Bosnian assembly in 1991, when you told the delegates that your view was this was a battle for -- this was a threat to Serbian living space.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I probably meant they were a threat as a military power, as an armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was your position, Mr. Kupresanin, that Bosnian Serb forces should conquer territories on which the Bosnian Serbs were a minority but on which they were a minority because of the genocide committed in World War II; right? And you said that in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: What did I believe? I believed that we were the left-overs of peoples who -- whose throats were cut during World War II and we would not allow that genocide over the Serbian people to be repeated. What the Jews in Germany had lived through is the same thing that we lived through in Croatia, in Bosnia, and other parts of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down and repeat this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat that I said that the Serbian people in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina after the world war, were the remains of a people whose throats had been cut, and we had to mobilise ourselves to the maximum to prevent further crimes against the Serbian people. And through our activity in the party, we did prevent it, at least temporarily. And raising the awareness among the people for -- in my eyes was an obligation. I repeat to you: In Croatia before the Second World War, there was a 1.900.000 Serbs. When the Second World War was over, there were 700.000 Serbs in Croatia. Communists came into power and they were not interested in that story. Nobody investigated it. A list of a highly-ranking German officer's -- a letter from -- high German officer said the Croats had cut the throats of 300.000 Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin. Mr. Kupresanin, I'm not asking you for dissertation on what happened in World War II, please. You --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And by -- for the Court's benefit and for the benefit of the parties, that was a reference -- the previous question was a reference to D456, pages 24 through 25 in the English and B/C/S, 27 through 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one comment, Mr. Tieger, about the exhibits. In your cross, first part of your cross-examination, we admitted 65 ter 32152, some part of pages -- some pages into Exhibit P6509, but I take it that exhibit is part of the associated exhibits which were admitted in its entirety as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe -- I understand the Court's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will vacate that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to say I -- I believe that that -- the -- the recording of that session it was comprised of a number of different, separate recordings and P -- I can't remember the exact number for the earlier referenced one may not comprise this particular excerpt I've referred to. I can double check on that, of course, but I suspect that's why I -- I just can't recall specifically. That's why it was separately referenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this the document about which Mr. Robinson rose to state, to admit in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I certainly have no objection if the -- in keeping with our previous practice with regard to similar sessions, if we aggregated the entirety of the transcripts referring to that particular session and introduced them just as we have introduced whole sessions of assembly sessions. That would seem consistent to me, so I couldn't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that this is only 20-page document, we will admit it in its entirety. And, therefore, as such, we will vacate the exhibit number of P6509. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, you also stated in 1994 that you personally think that Bosnia has always been a Serbian land and in that state there could not be three masters; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I always stated that Serbs, Orthodox Serbs, Muslim Serbs and Croatian Serbs lived in Bosnia. That's the way I see it, and that's the way it is. So if all of them are Serbs of various religious, according to this logic Bosnia is also a Serbian land. The synonym for a people is not the religion but the language that they speak. They all speak the Serbian language. And that's not what I said 150 or 200 years ago, Vuk Karadzic said it. The Muslim Serbs, the Catholic Serbs and the Orthodox Serbs all speak the Serbian language and the Stokavian dialect. The other dialects Kajkavian and Chakavian is the Slovenians who speak. Some Serbs also lived --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we have strayed away from the question. So your explanation is: You said that and now you've explained that what you meant was that the -- the Muslims are Muslim Serbs and so there can't be three masters --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- that the Serbs must be the masters. Okay. You also stated in January of 1993 --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I didn't say Serbs. They could be Muslims as Serbs, they are Serbs for me, all other facts do not support that. Everything else is a lie. Everything else is a communist division. There is no fact testifying that the Muslims are not Serbs. A million facts testify to it that Muslims are Serbs. Everything else is a lie, if we take facts as facts. Ninety per cent of the Croats are Serbs, Serbs who were converted to Catholicism, and those who were converted said: We are not Serbs, we are Croats now. As Slavs it's logical that we were converted to Christianity from the Byzantium and most of the Bosnian Muslims were converted to Islam from the Turks. So the majority of the Serbs were converted to Catholicism. They accepted it, especially during Maria Theresa, the queen. And now we are discussing who is who in these areas. The scientific elite in Europe knows who is who, and so does the Serbian scientific elite that is not communist.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please slow down. He's way too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, you're purporting now that you don't make any distinction between Muslims, Croats and Serbs for purposes of this discussion because to you they are all the same. But in January of 1993, after an immense amount of displacement, forcible displacement, killing and ethnic cleansing took place, you said the following, you said at 24th assembly session on the 8th of January, 1993: "We say that the war was not necessary in Bosnia and Herzegovina," referring to what some other people had said. And you said: "The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was necessary. Right now, if we were to count the population right now, there would be over a million Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnian-Herzegovina would be predominantly a Serb republic." And then to make the point completely clear, you said: "Is war necessary in Serbia? It's a horrible thing to say that the war would be necessary in Serbia. If Serbia does not go into the war now, then in three to five years, the Albanians and Muslims will legally overtake the power in Belgrade along with the Serb opposition. This war was necessary for the Serb people." So there you're making a clear distinction between Muslims and Serbs and you're asserting that without this war, there be too many Muslims who would soon be in a demographic position to legally overtake power; correct? That was your position in 1993.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I know that I said at rallies always that the Muslims are the Serbs. What I told the international representative, Stoltenberg, from Norway only confirmed my opinion. I'm saying that Albanians -- all Albanians are Albanians regardless of their religion because they speak the Albanian language which means that you have Orthodox Albanians, Catholic and Muslim Albanians. Likewise, there are Serbs of various religious. Only that here, there is this confusion of positions depending on what suits the international community.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, could you speak very slowly, please? The interpreters have difficulty following you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move on to another portion of your statement, Mr. Kupresanin. At several points in your statement, you attempt to emphasise alleged ARK power and independence. At paragraph 40 you said they were independent; at paragraph 42, you said -- that's vis-a-vis the municipalities, by the way. And let me put that another way so that I -- I -- so we don't have any confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please see the statement or, rather, be given the statement in hard copy so that he could follow and check what he has been asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, paragraph 40 you said the municipal Crisis Staffs were independent from the Krajina Crisis Staff. At paragraph -- that's right in the middle of that page. And at paragraph 42, you suggested that the ARK Crisis Staff was more of a Banja Luka-specific Crisis Staff. So that's what you say now about the powers of the ARK Crisis Staff vis-a-vis the municipalities or the role of the Crisis Staff vis-a-vis the municipalities. But back in 2001, you said that that was a big mystery to you, and let me turn your attention to page 33 of the English and page 46 of the B/C/S. This is --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Brdjanin give orders to presidents of municipalities about what he wanted carried out? And you said, Well, you see, I -- I ask myself that question. Certain things happened in Krajina. I'm interested to what extent was the ARK Crisis Staff connected to the peripheral -- question: Municipal Crisis Staffs. And your answer, Yes, yes, that is a great mystery for me. And yet now, a dozen years later, after meeting with the Karadzic Defence, you suddenly claim that that mystery is no mystery at all and you can state that there -- to the contrary, that -- that it had no role with the municipal Crisis Staffs; right? You changed your position completely, haven't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Do you expect me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of a single institution in Republika Srpska which ordered that Crisis Staffs be formed by regions. That Crisis Staff which was established in the region was not established at the order of the government of Republika Srpska, so I believed it to be unlawful. The government of Republika Srpska ordered the establishment of Crisis Staffs by municipalities. Banja Luka is a municipality, did not establish a Crisis Staff at the time, nor did it have one. The Crisis Staff of Krajina had no members from Krajina. All the people in the Krajina Crisis Staff hailed from Banja Luka. So that for me, the Krajina Crisis Staff was a -- rather a Crisis Staff of Banja Luka. I also assert that in the communication between the Crisis Staff of Krajina in Banja Luka and the municipality in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, there practically was no communication, as the Crisis Staff had no subordination either vertical or horizontal. The Crisis Staff cannot punish, didn't have its account, and it all means that the Crisis Staff is some sort of a body or institution of a preventive character in a situation when people feel that there could be some kind of danger from a natural disaster to war. The Crisis Staff has the task to promote and establish a rule of law, if that is possible, in the area where it is situated, so that I can note that each municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, that's -- this is not -- okay, I need to interrupt you. This is not a platform for you to make dissertations on these subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will add this page to P6510.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, although you said it was a big mystery to you in 2001, the fact is that contemporaneous documents from the municipalities completely contradict your assertion here now that there was no level of hierarchy between the ARK Crisis Staff and the municipalities. For example -- and let me ask you about Bosanski Novi. P2632. This Court has received evidence that the Bosanski Novi Crisis Staff, in reporting on its work, referred to implementing the ARK decision on disarmament, also referred to the ARK decision on general public mobilisation, and stated: "After familiarising themselves with such a decision of the ARK government, the Crisis Staff initiated concrete actions and tasked organs in charge with implementing the decision." So do you claim you're unfamiliar with Novi's position on their relationship to the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I didn't know anything. I didn't know anything about these relations and co-ordinations, nor could the Crisis Staff of the ARK Krajina influence the way that the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Novi would act. It did not have such force. It did not have such powers. There was no possibility for the Crisis Staff to do something, nor could it do anything according to the law and nobody was due to obey it. I'm not aware of this kind of communication.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If we ask witness to put off headphones or not to be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you going to make some objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I would like to make objections that can't wait for the redirect. All things that are cited are selective and wrongly posed questions that do not fit with the material that is cited. For example, on page 53, line 33 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. I think we can continue. Yes. If could you take off your headphone for the moment, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I don't hear anything then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a procedural issue so it's better for you not to hear it. [In English] On 33, line 33: "I'm telling you that the Crisis Staffs in municipalities were Gods, they were a state within a state, and they acted differently in each municipality." And on 26, page 26, line 50, 51, and 52: "Well, I didn't say or I didn't mention something that is very important in all of this, all the most important things of all this. The Crisis Staffs in the municipalities were states and presidents of municipalities and presidents of the Executive Councils were the leaders, all communication between civilian and military authorities were through these people." So I think that there would be no witness who wouldn't be confused by this kind of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow your objections. Mr. Tieger this time clearly showed -- cited some part of the prior record. Where is it from, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P2632, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although it was not shown to the witness, I think it was fair enough to cite that part and put to the witness about his observation. Let us continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, I object also that Mr. Tieger testifies and is not interested in response from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will monitor, but so far we can continue. But I -- in the future, we would be more benefited if you showed the document to the witness and then ask a comment on that. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's call up 3497, please. P3497, English page 1, B/C/S page 2. Public announcement of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Kljuc on the 8th of May, 1992, stating among other things: "All decisions shall be made and tasks performed in compliance with the regulations and decisions of the organs of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the Serbian Republic of BiH."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it you were unfamiliar with that position of the Kljuc Crisis Staff as well? And the portion I read out is in the second paragraph in B/C/S, sir.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: This Crisis Staff in Krajina, I think that they simply usurped power. That's my opinion. There is a time for a Crisis Staff to exist, and when the war breaks out, then the War Presidencies should take over the authority, then the Ministry of the Defence, the Ministry of the Interior, they should do their work. I'm not sure according to what logic the Crisis Staff was doing that after the breakout of the war. It should do its duties in peacetime, when there is a premonition that war might be coming or if there is a natural disaster. So, for me, this is pure usurpation. But probably this kind of communication did exist, though I don't see any stamp here. The Crisis Staff of the Kljuc municipality did not have a stamp. It doesn't have a stamp, which means that no Crisis Staff had a stamp or a giro account. It wasn't a legal entity, and it's decisions were not to be taken into account. Someone who is in war and needs to communicate with the municipalities is the ministry of arm -- of the army or the command of the army. This is somebody who is infiltrating an empty space and doing some business. And what I say in the end is that that means usurping power.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And according to you, irrespective of the communication between the ARK Crisis Staff and the municipal Crisis Staffs, that there was nevertheless a chain of command running from the municipalities clear up to Dr. Karadzic, and that's what you said back in 2001; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I would exclude the Crisis Staff from any real operation if the rule of law existed. There was no Crisis Staff at the level of Republika Srpska, as far as I know. That was why a Crisis Staff is unusual. It has no subordination or co-ordination from top to bottom or from bottom to top either. So someone infiltrates himself. During wartime, subordination and co-ordination are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's set the Crisis Staff aside for the moment. Your position in 2001 was that there was a chain of command conducted through the presidents of the municipalities through to the president of the state. That is Dr. Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent the president of the municipality is in communication with the president of the country. There is some different kind of communication during the war, when war is at issue. If it's the president of the municipality, he probably tried to co-operate with the political leadership of the republic which is logical, but whether that was the rule, that depends on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this is what you said in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 27 of the English, lines 9 through 15, and page 38 of the Serbian, lines 1 through 7: "They -- then the other kind of communication was then conducted from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until we have the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry. Did I fail to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Actually, here there was a double command in existence. The civilian authorities were directed at the President of Republika Srpska and the military authorities were focused on the commander, General Mladic. There was no co-ordination and subordination, but, rather, double authorities, just like a double stake is not put into earth. So that Radovan Karadzic had control. He had the state, but he did not have the power; and the army had the power but didn't have the state. So the army used us purely for logistics, but we didn't have much influence. And if crimes happened in certain areas, then civilians were not killing civilians. It was some army or paramilitary formations that were doing that. In Republika Srpska we had military courts and military prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's stick to the subject. So what you were confirming there was your, quote: "They -- then the other kind of communication was then conducted from the presidents of the municipalities, through the chain of command, to the president of the state of the country. And then military people, they have their own chain of command, which also ended, went to the top, to the Supreme Commander, General Mladic." That's what you said in 2001; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I said that it was double command. The hierarchy in a state is well known. What if the American president ordered a ship of the sixth US fleet to fire at a town, and if they refused to obey the order, you know what would happen. In our country, such orders could not be issued. There was very often obstruction --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question was a simple one. And in connection with -- before we break -- with that, one more thing. When were you asked about Brdjanin's authority and whether he could order the police or the military to do certain tasks, you responded in the following way and let's turn to page 43 of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're tendering page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be added to P6510.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And page 43 of the English, lines [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? May I say what you said, just to confirm or to reject it? Mr. Brdjanin could not order anything to anyone. He could only make suggestions but not to order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A question will be asked after taking a look at the document first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 43 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just -- may I just clarify? Who is AC who formulates the question in lines 2 to 5 in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can see at the bottom of the page usually. Let us see whether we have it. Yes, you should have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have nothing. I don't have any AC. Those are the initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see it under the AC.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There are -- I -- if we could -- okay. There are four people listed: Mr. Kupresanin, two people from the Office of the Prosecutor, and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Back to what --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not there in the English version. In the English version there is only three, and I have the English version in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's safe to say that this was conducted through an interpreter. And the fact that it's contained in the Serbian version should be adequate, and this is [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On this English page there is no AC. That's why. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again page 43 of the English and page 63 of the Serbian, lines 11 through 12 in the Serbian, and 11 through 16 in the English, you were asked as -- and you just mentioned something about Brdjanin's authority to order the police or the military to do certain tasks. Question was: "What was the authority? Would he order? Could he order the police or the military to do certain tasks?" You said: "He could have ordered naive policemen and naive army or military. They were all listening to Radovan's orders." And that's what you said in 2001 about who had the authority over the military and police and who could order them to conduct tasks; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Even a layman would know that it was the Ministry of Police that gave orders to the police and that the Ministry of Defence, through the Supreme Commander and military commanders, issued orders. Brdjanin, the Crisis Staff, could not issue any orders to anyone. So it's logical that people should know that the Supreme Commander and the commander of that army could issue orders and exclude the Crisis Staff from the sphere of power, some power. I said naive. Yes, he could issue orders only to the naive, the Crisis Staff -- many did not obey the Crisis Staff at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, I tender that excerpt, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will issue -- we will consider this together with the other pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I see it's time for the break. And again I just emphasise in circumstances where there is a straightforward adoption of the prior statement, I have no problem with that, of course. And in the sense in which that's a prior consistent statement, we are perfectly in agreement with Mr. Robinson, but where there is equivocation I think these -- the prior statement is -- should -- should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If I could put something on the record with respect to our associated exhibits at the request of the Registrar. And that is that our document 70, 65 ter 17367 is, in fact, subsumed in 65 ter 17356 and need not be admitted, and then the intercept which is 30061 which had the wrong participants is not being tendered and being withdrawn. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a second. We will come back to this issue about the associated exhibits. We will resume at 1.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, during the break the Chamber has reviewed all the pages shown to the witness, and the Chamber is of the view that all those pages were not entirely consistent with the witness's evidence and on that ground we will admit them all. Those pages will be added to the Exhibit P6510.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, I wanted to turn next to paragraph 22 of your statement. That deals with a -- the minutes of a session of the ARK assembly in November 1991, and reflects your comments that you insisted on the replacement of directors of companies and institutions and the appointment of SDS staff in their stead but Dr. Karadzic was for harmony and unity and insisted that the old staffs remain in their positions. Now, first of all, as a general matter, it is correct to say that in the ARK, a great many dismissals took place and that task was carried out by the Executive Council of Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Are you asking me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: The Serb Democratic Party won the elections in Banja Luka that year, and it is to be expected -- and it's to be expected that people from the Serbian Democratic Party would take key positions in companies, especially state-owned companies, or, rather, public companies. That is logical. That is to be expected. Why else did the SDS take part in the elections? We took part in the elections because we thought that we were better than those who were there beforehand, and I don't think there was anything bad in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thanks. And I wasn't trying to make --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I have to finish. Do allow me to finish. It is correct that Mr. Karadzic insisted that we do not dismiss the directors. He insisted on that many times in order to create some kind of peace, harmony et cetera and I said these are communist directors and they should go, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please follow the question. The first question was not asking you to make a value judgement either way about dismissals or to tell me who instigated those dismissals. It was just to confirm the fact that it was the case that in the Krajina, a great many dismissals ultimately took place and that the Executive Council of Krajina carried out that task. And do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, there was a replacement of communist cadres, in part to a large degree. I'm not saying totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, let me -- and more specifically, you -- with respect to the ARK Crisis Staff and Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Brdjanin pushed very hard to have people who were not Serbs dismissed from important positions, in fact, all positions at any higher level in companies, and that, in fact, many -- there were great changes in response to that, and it was the Executive Council of Krajina that carried out that task?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that there was this purge, if you will, of these other peoples in the Krajina. There were probably replacements because the SDS won the election and then their people took key positions. I keep repeating that. Like in Sarajevo, where the SDA won and then the key positions were held by SDA people. So who prevented Serbs from being members of the SDA? They would have then gotten key positions in Sarajevo just like here. If the Muslims were in the SDS then they -- had they joined it, then they could have been in the same position because the statute of the SDS says that the SDS is the party of the Serb people and other peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to 65 ter 25608 once again, English page 58, and B/C/S 85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, you are advised to speak slow. Please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in July of 2001 you were asked, Brdjanin also pushed very hard to have people who were not Serbs dismissed from important positions, in fact all positions at any higher level in companies; is that correct? And you said, There were great changes carried out at that time. I can't say that there were not many great changes. The Executive Council of Krajina carried out this task. You have signatures of people who were dismissed. And then it was said, Yes. Brdjanin's signature. And you said, Very well, everything is clear. That's what you said in 2001, correct, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that case I think it's best to tender the excerpt, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to take a closer look at the document you cite in paragraph 22, that's P551 -- 5551, let's call that up, please. That's an extract from the minutes of the 9th session of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina which was held on the 6th of November, 1991. Looking at item 1, it states that it was established that the presidents of municipalities had failed to fully carry out the conclusions we adopted together at the last session. And it goes on to point out that in some places it was impossible to implement those conclusions because they could only be carried out within the party and notes that Brdjanin should inform Dr. Karadzic about this level of implementation. Now, the agenda also refers to the implementation -- at the beginning refers to the implementation of conclusions adopted at the session held on the 26th of October 1991. So those conclusions that had not been fully carried out that were just discussed related back to the 26th of October, 1991. Now, we know from that date that that was the day of the Sarajevo SDS order. Let's look at 2548, please. All right. So this is the document which reflects the order which was brought to light at the meeting of the presidents of municipalities held on the 26th of October, 1991, in Banja Luka, and which was chaired by Dr. Karadzic and at which the conclusion were fully accepted by the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And if you look down the list, it includes, in part, to take over power in public firms, post office, account keeping institution, administration of justice, and especially in mass communication media. So, Mr. Kupresanin, in contrast to the suggestion you make in paragraph 22 about the significance of the document P5551, at that time, Dr. Karadzic, in fact, was urging, indeed ordering, the replacement of the cadres deemed unacceptable to the SDS in particular position -- in important positions in public firms and other important institutions; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, of course, the SDS should have its own people in public companies. That is quite logical. If other people who are suspicious stay on, they could create great problems. There were some Croats and Muslims in key positions and then the transportation of weapons took place all the time, to Croatia where there was a war between the Serbs and Croats; that is to say, these were not trustworthy people. We were very sensitive because we knew what was happening and we knew what would happen. We expected problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is quite logical for us to appoints our own people. What's so sinful about that? I think it's a good thing that that was done, to put one's own cadres not those of other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look at another reflection of the emphasis on replacing personnel in important positions in the Bosnian institutions and especially in mass communication media, and if we could turn to 65 ter 32823, please, this is an intercepted telephone conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Vukic around the same time, that is around the fall of 1991. This is September 27th, 1991. And if we turn to the second page of the document, please, in both languages, and it will continue in the Serbian. Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Vukic are talking, and Dr. Karadzic says, In whose hands is radio Banja Luka? And Vukic says, I beg your pardon? Karadzic, In whose hands is radio Banja Luka? Vukic: A Muslim is a director. Karadzic: What the fuck? Vukic: Shall I replace him straight away, let him go to fucking hell? Karadzic: Come on replace him immediately. Appoint a man of yours. These are war times. Appoint -- if he is not listening to you, appoint a man of yours -- not listening. If he is not listening to you and is sabotaging, appoint a man of yours. Then he goes on to ask who the main editor is and is pointed out that her ethnicity is Serbian and she is a woman. Now, that's another reflection, is it not, Mr. Kupresanin, of the effort by Dr. Karadzic, contrary to your suggestion in paragraph 22, to ensure the replacement of personnel deemed inappropriate with personnel acceptable to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: May I start answering? The director of radio Banja Luka that belonged to the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the director was a Muslim. The director was not a Muslim it was Rajko Vasic. I remember that very well. There was this Svetlana who was the editor. But it is true that there was a man who was a Muslim, and this television -- I cannot remember his last name now, maybe I will remember. We replaced Rajko Vasic. Not this man who was there, who was of the Muslim faith. We did not have any problems with him. We did not attack him at all. It was this Rajko Vasic, who was our problem, a Serb. We did not touch the Muslim at all. And this Muslim testified here in The Hague, as far as I can remember, in relation to what happened during the war and the Krajina. So what's bad about that? It is bad that we replaced people who were working in television? In Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had these televisions that were all anti-Serbs, Yutel, TV Zagreb, and I personally do not mind having people dismissed or replaced. I was replaced, too, on television, proposal of the SDS, President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that and obviously be -- I shouldn't say obviously, but I assume it would be MFI'd unless there is agreement to the contrary by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P6509, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, Mr. Kupresanin, to the crimes that took place in the Krajina and particularly during 1992. Now, there was no mystery about that, was there? I mean, there were many, many crimes which took place and you were aware of them at the time or shortly after they happened; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, it's been a very long time, for me to find out about a crime. I mean, the crime committed at Koricanske Stijene, first of all, people started whispering about that and then that went on for months, and then I finally found out the truth. So television was probably concealing that. Sometimes these media companies who were supposed to provide information for some reason provided misinformation. So as for many crimes, I did not find out about them quickly and no one sent me information like that. To be quite frank, I heard about Prijedor too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kupresanin, back in 2001, you explained that many bad things happened in Krajina and you would find out about those things about 15 or 20 days after something had happened. And, indeed, you'd find out from regular people, from Muslims and Croats, and specifically you found out about Omarska about 15 days afterwards, that is after it was formed. That's all true, right, that's what you said in 2001?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No, no. I found out about Omarska when President Karadzic called me and he asked me to ask people in Prijedor to disband that reception centre. For me that was a reception centre, not a camp, and that's what I did. That was the time when I found out about that. How many days had elapsed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what you knew or claimed to know in 2001. If we could turn back to 25608, to English page 22, and B/C/S page 31. And at lines 32 or 31 you begin to say, As far as I know, many bad things happened in Krajina but I never knew anything about it. I would find out about it only 15 or 20 days after something happened. And I would find out about those things from Muslims and Croats and regular people, ordinary people. And then toward the bottom of that -- toward the end of that answer you say at lines 39 through 41 in the English, For example, there is camp in Omarska, and 15 days I didn't know what -- for 15 days I didn't know about it. I was informed about it by relatives of Muslims or Croats. That's what you said in 2001, isn't it, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: For example, if something happened in the territory of Krajina, well, specifically concerning Croats, let's say, Bishop Komarica would immediately come to my office and ask me to participate in inquiring into that. And every time he asked, I went to inquire on the spot. That's one type of information. Or, for instance, Emir Pusatlic [phoen], a dentist, when an incident happened, when there was a problem, he would come to my office. It would be some serious Muslim connection. He would let me know and see if we could intervene. So that was this non-Serb connection. And the Serb connection would be a request from Radovan Karadzic for me to go to Omarska and do that job. So that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be added too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Bishop Komarica and other people. Let me -- let me ask you about a specific example of crimes that you found out about. You found out about the mass killing in the village of Bresevo, where the Bosnian Serb army entered the village and killed, according to what you learned, 68 people in July; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I heard about it from Bishop Komarica. I didn't hear it from a different source. He asked me to go to the scene and find out how much of it is true. So we went. There were two military men with us. They drove us. And we entered Brisevo village. It's not Bresevo, it's Brisevo. We came to a different village which had a little Catholic church. And when we came, there were some women there. Komarica held a mass service. These women were moaning and asking us to enable them, if we possibly can, to leave that village. We tried to tell them different -- suggested different options, but they wouldn't listen. Now, how many people were killed, I don't know. I don't know your figure is correct. In one variant is 88, another variant is 63, and there are different figures. I was very willing to help, together with Bishop Komarica, and Mr. Karadzic never held it against me that I made these efforts and he always encouraged me, on the contrary, and told me that I need to look after other ethnic communities. Usually, the president of the SDS, Krzic, came; president of the HDZ, Gabelic; Catholic priests; hodzas; Muslim intellectuals, came to my office, came to speak to me as if there were no war going on. And I tried to help them all, and I did all I could with the encouragement and approval of President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you learned about this terrible crime in Brisevo? Did you keep it to yourself or did you tell someone in the republic-level authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I found out from Mr. Komarica the first time. Now, whether I informed anyone, we had two military persons who kept a record and of course they were supposed to submit a report to the military authorities because the perpetrator was the army. I know that I discussed this with several people and I'm sure that I discussed it with a member of the Presidency, Biljana Plavsic. I was much closer to her than to other people. Ideologically we were close. The others looked to me a bit like communists, left of centre, or leftist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also told Mr. Karadzic and you also told --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness also said whereas the two of us were monarchists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure I said Krajisnik. I discussed it in detail with Biljana Plavsic, as a member of the Presidency, not Karadzic. That's the one thing that I'm sure about. I'm not sure about the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 6 should say "Krajisnik" instead of "Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's right. That's certainly -- yeah, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn back to what you said in 2001 when these events were fresher in your mind. And if we could turn to page 62 of 65 ter 25608, and page 92 of the B/C/S. Question, this begins at page -- line 39 of the English: "Okay, Mr. Kupresanin, my question is: When people informed you about the crimes that were committed on them, what was your response to those crimes, the killings and the destruction of their property?" You said: "Well, what I heard there I told the others. It didn't stay with me or -- "Q. Who did you inform, who did you inform?" And you said: "For example, Momo Krajisnik, maybe a certain number of ministers, all deputies from here." Then it continues on to the next page in English, and same page in Serbian, and you discuss how quickly according to the victims this occurred, which brigade may have been involved, and then later we see you say, No, I informed -- you didn't inform General Talic but no, I informed ministers, minister of the army. It was Nikolic, I don't know, or it was Subotic. And the question was: "So you're saying whoever was the minister of defence at that time, the RS minister for defence, you brought this information to his knowledge?" And the answer is, That was the schedule. That was how you do things. So, in fact, that's who you recalled were among the people to whom you reported this crime after you learned about it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, okay, I was informed and I probably informed some other people. I don't remember. I don't think that was within my competence. I think it was within the competence of military courts and military prosecutor's offices that were in operation at the time in Republika Srpska. I had only two military men around me and on all my travels and contacts with other ethnic communities and priests and hodzas, those militaries were present, for the most part, and it was logical for them to inform their commands, Talic and the others. That was not my job. But because the crime had happened, I told people. That I know 100 per cent that I had spoken to Biljana Plavsic. About the others, I'm not sure. It's possible that I spoke to the minister of the army as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also said - and that's found at page 63 of the English, again same page in Serbian - many people, even if they heard that, they didn't want to hear about it. That was your experience in attempting to report these things, wasn't it, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, there were many situations when specifically the government was not willing to do its job and they were not interested. I had problems, and when I informed them they don't want to get involved. They don't want to share in it. We know exactly who was in charge. Who perpetrated the murders. We know exactly who perpetrated the crime. It's quite sure that within one hour all the perpetrators could have been identified, and later prosecuted and held responsible. I was a deputy. It was not my job. But it is human to react as much as I could within my limitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And despite those efforts, those people who were known were not arrested and prosecuted at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I know that it's not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: They didn't do their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to turn next to paragraph 60, in which you assert that there were no organised expulsions. So that's the position that you take in your statement. But back in 2001, your position was a bit different. Then, you were asked about ways of making the Muslims and Croats leave the area, and you indicated that you knew the municipalities did that and said it was on their own initiative but then went on to say, Well, maybe that's not the case. Maybe there was someone who co-ordinated it. Does that refresh your recollection about the occurrence of organised efforts to expel Muslims and the fact that you were not prepared to say at that time -- first of all, you thought the municipality -- you were -- you knew that the municipalities did it and you considered that maybe there was someone who co-ordinated it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, I was a deputy in the assembly of Republika Srpska. There was never any activity in that direction or was such a project of expulsion ever advocated. I was a member of the board and never was there any activity in that direction. But I have to be frank and honest, municipalities in Republika Srpska were states unto themselves and there was no co-ordination whatsoever. For instance I was in Krajina. I didn't know what was going on in Prijedor. I -- I didn't know what was going on in Brisevo. I didn't know what was going on in Koricanske Stijene. I cannot say I ever encountered an incident wherein people would be expelled at gunpoint. I know that people left so as to avoid military service and because of poverty and deprivation. Nobody prohibited it, and there is a Geneva Convention on the freedom of movement and it allows people to move out and go wherever they like. There was Sarajevo where people could not leave. So all of them lived in a ghetto, just to prove the democracy of Alija Izetbegovic, and we all know how they fared.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's go back to paragraph 60. So if I understand you correctly you are not in a position to assert -- that you cannot assert that it is not true that there was an active and systematic repression and expulsion of Muslims. You can only say at this point that you don't know everything that was going on, that's the most you can say, you're willing to say now. But, in fact, in 2001 you said you knew that the municipalities were doing that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, I can say about the municipalities where I physically moved around, I am from the Banja Luka municipality and I know that nobody was expelled there, from Laktasi either. I was in Prnjavor, in some Muslim villages in 1995. And in that municipality, in those villages, specifically Muslim villages, I worked as a teacher and I went there to visit my Muslim friends. I found them, they had never moved anywhere, and they told me, The Serb authorities are treating us quite well. So in 1995, in August, I was there. In August 1995, the Muslims were there. And there were charges against --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear against whom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the expulsions of Muslims from Prijedor. In other municipalities, I was not physically present, and I could not make anyone send me daily reports. So I maintain that the political leadership was not doing that. It was not the political position of the top leadership or the assembly. But it's possible that some municipalities did it. And it's very viable. It can be checked. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 2, page 85, the interpreters didn't hear properly. The witness said I was deputy to the Main Board of the party, and at the beginning of page 85, the witness enumerated municipalities, Srbac, where he comes from, Laktasi, Banja Luka, Prnjavor and Gradiska. These are municipalities where he knows nobody was expelled from. Maybe there are some more municipalities that he mentioned, but these did not find their way into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have noticed the buses, the people being expelled, the police. I didn't see that. I only saw buses carrying prisoners from Manjaca. There was an organised convoy of buses headed by police cars and I saw that they were escorting someone. And I asked who and they told me prisoners from Manjaca. But in those municipalities where I was able to move around and visit, nobody was expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's just as a final -- focus on this topic, let's turn to page 36 of your 2001 interview, in the English, and page 52 at the bottom and 53 at the very top of the Serbian. And at the bottom of the page in English, beginning at line 41, you're asked, Did the Crisis Staff, again referring to the ARK Crisis Staff, discuss ways of making the Muslims and Croats leave this area of the Krajina? Your answer, I don't think so. I know that municipalities did that on their own initiative but maybe it's -- maybe that's not the case. Maybe there was someone who co-ordinated it. That's what you said in 2001; right, Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I said "maybe, maybe" everywhere. I told you roughly the truth about the areas where I moved around. I told you that the top leadership of Republika Srpska, the political leadership, never pursued that, never pursued any activity wherein people would be physically expelled and we would remain alone in these areas. As to what happened in municipalities, I don't know what happened in some other municipalities such as Novi. I know that Pasic had certain problems. I know that much. I know they had problems. But who else? I don't know. I know about Kotor Varos. There were problems. I participated in Kotor Varos on another project.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that excerpt, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned Kotor Varos. Very quickly, what you said when you went there was -- you were told the presidents of the local communes that the Serb army has tanks and guns, and that you don't have the right to sacrifice your children. So let's try to find some solution; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Right. I received on a daily basis information from the ground, from the municipality of Kotor Varos, where heinous crimes occurred. People were impaled, they were murdered, some people were even roasted on a spit, if you can imagine that. I don't know in whose minds this idea was born, but this was done by the Muslims and the Serbs were killed in various ways. And then Bishop Komarica came to see me, I told him horrible things are happening in Kotor Varos, let's do something about it, and he said, Vojo, I'm at your disposal. Then I contacted two Catholic priests in Kotor Varos and one hodza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not so much interested at the moment in the details of your activities in Kotor Varos at that time. I wanted to focus on your position regarding the relative military weaponry available and your comment that it was the Serb army that had tanks and guns. So I wanted to ask you if it was not the case that you were always adamant, from the beginning of the war to the end, that the Serbs were vastly superior militarily to the Muslims and, in particular, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Well, it was true, we had weapons. It was true we were able to commit crimes. Now, combatting the Muslim and Croat army was not a crime. However, there were hundreds of children there who were innocent. I made an appeal. I told them, You don't have the right to kill your children. I am at your disposal. I offered this, this, this and this. But it's true they were -- they had tanks, they had webers, they he had howitzers, they were able to do the job, and a lot of Muslims and Serbs eventually were killed in that operation. But the purpose was to save lives, but primarily the children. So we -- we carried out that project, Mr. Komarica and I. Sometimes policy is stronger than all the howitzers in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have limited amount of time left so I wanted to turn to paragraph 46 of your statement, Mr. Kupresanin, where you state that the local -- you discuss among other things Omarska and Keraterm and you state that the authorities, local authorities in Prijedor, acted on their own initiative there. Now, that's not consistent with what you said back in 2001. In 2001, you said, in fact, you were interested to know who ordered the establishing of the camp in Omarska. If you turn to page 37 of the English of the 2001 interview and page 53 of the B/C/S, and then in a related excerpt at page 62 -- page 42 of the English and page 62 of the B/C/S, there you're referring to, at the beginning, your effort to get Mevludin Sejmenovic out of Omarska, which you say you did on your own initiative, but then you say: I want to say that Radovan Karadzic told me personally that he had nothing to do with that, but my feeling is - what I have is - that the order about the camp, about the camps to be established, didn't come from Brdjanin but somewhere, someone on the top, but I don't know who from. So back in 2001, Mr. Kupresanin, it was your position that you thought that the Omarska camp, that you didn't -- first of all, you said you didn't -- you were interested to know who ordered it, and that you thought the order had come from somewhere on the top but you didn't know. So your statement in -- in paragraph 46 that it was a local initiative is belied by what you said in 2001 when these events were fresher in your memory; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I can say, at the time when you were interviewing me, I did not have the real picture. Now, after all this time that has passed, I gave it a lot of thought. What actually happened in Prijedor? Two or three days before the conflict in Prijedor, people from Prijedor and people from Omarska came. They asked the president of the Executive Board, that is to say the prime minister of Krajina, to enable them and find a way --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, just -- okay. First of all, just so we get a -- are you relating now what you knew at the time or what you've learned since?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I'm telling you the real truth and please hear me out. So two or three days before this clash in Prijedor, people came from Omarska and from Prijedor. Omarska is a place in the Prijedor municipality. The delegation from Omarska asked that the municipality be divided into two municipalities, Prijedor and Omarska. Why? Because of the Ljubija mine. Ljubija is a mine that yielded huge money. And people from Omarska were thinking that Prijedor is stealing from them, so they came to see the president of the Executive Board to talk to him about how to go about it, and he invited me to assist, to attend the meeting. So they asked me, too, What should we do to achieve this division? I didn't know the answer. Nikola didn't know the answer. So the conclusion is, two or three days before the conflict in Prijedor, the political leadership didn't know it would happen. That's my opinion. I believe the army knew but the political leadership of Republika Srpska did not know. And, again, I maintain that sometimes municipalities acted on their own. And in this case, the political leadership of Prijedor did not organise any conflicts or any clashes, and in the end it was the Muslims who attacked the municipality of Prijedor, not the political leadership of the municipality. I exclude the political leadership of the municipality and the republic but the army knew. The municipality was attacked. Some villages were attacked but it was all done by Muslim forces. They were the first to attack. So many people got killed in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You -- we have to finish up pretty quick. Do you know how many Muslims and Croats were in Omarska or Keraterm by the time of the attack on Prijedor town on the 31st of May, 1992? Do you know how many Muslims and Croats had already been rounded up from their homes and placed in one or either of these camps?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
