utterances.text: I don't know about Keraterm. I visited Omarska and I saw hundreds of people. A huge number of people were there. All these people were leaning against the fence or were sitting down on the asphalt. That was what I saw. I stood by these people, I spoke a few words with them, because I know that I got the task to have the camp disbanded and I came to do that. How many people were there? There were many, perhaps 1.000 or 800. I don't know. I think people kept arriving even after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there were --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: There were many people there. I don't know anything about Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Two more quick points about Omarska: First of all, you say, and you repeated it here a few minutes ago, that Dr. Karadzic called you and suggested you use your authority and ask the local authorities to close down Omarska. In fact, in 2001 you explained that Dr. Karadzic called you to visit the municipal authorities and tell them to dismiss the camp that day, and that day meant immediately after it had been discovered by the international community and been highly publicised. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No, that's not correct at all. I didn't say immediately. I said that President Karadzic said that it should be dismissed and that on the second day, when it was disbanded and when I went to Manjaca I entered the buildings and I gave to speech to these people. I told them that they would come to no harm and that only those who were guilty would be held to account. And I saw the facilities, and the facilities could not be put in order and adjusted for the needs. At least a month was necessary. These were huge buildings, so probably the camp had been prepared for 20 days or a month in order to be functional so that it could be used. That was my estimate. And no one ever said a single word that it had to be on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't tender the previous excerpts referred to which were pages 62 and 63 of the English and 92 and 93 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: English page numbers again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sixty-two and 63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And not this one? Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I haven't put that to -- I asked a general question. I haven't -- with respect to the answer the witness just gave, there is not a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, they will be added as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn quickly to page 37 in the English, page 54 in the B/C/S, and the lines -- relevant lines are 27 through 29 in the English, 8 through 10 in the B/C/S, where you relate to -- you see that there, Mr. Kupresanin? The line begins, I asked -- I asked one day Radovan Karadzic, and then it continues, And he asked me as a deputy to visit the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor and to tell them to dismiss the camp during that day. And you've also said that you and Dr. Karadzic got into a big argument about the camp on the phone. You see that excerpt, sir? B/C/S is 8 through -- look at line 8 through 10 toward the top of the page. That's what you said in 2001, that Dr. Karadzic asked you --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: All right. I know that Dr. Karadzic asked me to do this but he did not impose any deadlines. He didn't say I had to do it immediately. First of all, it's impossible to do it at once. He said see what the situation is like there and, please, as this was a camp through which inmates kept moving, ask the army to create the conditions so that people could live normally in the camp. But I don't remember that he said I should do it immediately. I came to Prijedor and found a great number of journalists there from various international agencies, such as Reuters, the BBC, and so on, and I believe that they were at the camp. They visited it at that day, and also visited the president of the municipality. There were so many journalists there. I found them in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that excerpt, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we saw that page before as well. We will add that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Kupresanin, I simply want you to confirm that while you were at Omarska, you spoke to Dr. Karadzic on the phone and that was in the presence of Mr. Sejmenovic, who you took out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: What have I heard? What am I supposed to say? What do you expect from me? I hear you real well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I notice in discussing what happened in Omarska your statement doesn't mention anything about Mr. Sejmenovic, anything about a telephone call to Dr. Karadzic in the presence of Mr. Sejmenovic, which was something that [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic told Mr. Sejmenovic didn't happen. In fact, it did happen. You did speak to Dr. Karadzic on the phone from Omarska in the general presence of Sejmenovic and then you took him out of the camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. I did not call anyone on the phone from Omarska. I came from Omarska, then I informed Radovan, and Sejmenovic was in my office at the time. Mr. Sejmenovic. I ordered half a litre of coffee as the Muslims drink a lot of coffee and I gave him two boxes of cigarettes. And I told Radovan, Mr. President, what is going on there? And he told me, Vojo, those fools and idiots, no one obeys me. It was to that effect. And it turned out that he had some idea about that, so perhaps I did not put this nicely, and perhaps he was even more rude when he said -- he said, Those guys there, those idiots, that was -- he said, which means my conclusion from the conversation with him was that Radovan had nothing do with it. But my conclusion was also that the political leadership of the Prijedor municipality also had nothing to do with it. My final conclusion was that the army oversaw all this. How would the political leadership of one municipality allow the Muslims to enter and kill so many Serbs, if they had been preparing anything, the Serbs were killed first and then all the other things developed as they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So there was no problem with the telephone lines and the man you spoke to from your office, from -- was Dr. Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I informed him what I had done. And throughout this time, Mevludin Sejmenovic sat next to me and he listened to what I was talking about. Only that this Mevludin, whom I treated as my own brother, was here at a trial in 1994 for the first time and he said the absolute truth about everything that he had seen, and it was absolute truth, and then he corrected his positions. He kept changing them, probably because he was persuaded by the political party that he's a member of, so that I am somewhat angry or rather quite angry at him because he was not fair and he was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So the Muslim you talked about is Mevludin Sejmenovic who testified in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Sejmenovic, S-e-j-m-e-n-o-v-i-c. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, a general question, Mr. Kupresanin. Do you remember whether you read the transcript of this interview dating from 2001? Did you read it then? Was it given to you to read it over and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I don't understand you. Please, can you explain. What transcript, whose transcript? With regard to whom and what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interview which Mr. Tieger showed and cited many pages. When this interview was conducted, did you receive it for inspection and for reading it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No. He took the statute of the autonomous region from me, I signed each page, and whatever I had with regard to your abolitions of Muslims and Croats. Any documents I had they seized it from me. I had no copies so I was left without it and without the statute of Krajina. I delivered everything over to ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the interview itself was audio-taped. Did you receive it later on to read it and to sign it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please show page 39? You said a little while ago that you called me from your office and Mr. Tieger suggested that it was from Omarska. Let's see what you said about that in 2001.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I think I said that I called you from my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, please, have a look at 39 in English and I'm not sure which page of the Serbian version. The page in English is 39. I'm going to read it out.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Please read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From line 4, question: [In English] "When you were in the Omarska camp did you talk to Karadzic from the camp by telephone?"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serbian 55, [Interpretation] 56 in Serbian. Let me just read it out. I will read out your answer and you will get it on the screen as well. But this is your answer in English: [In English] "When I returned to the office, that's when I had this verbal conflict with him, and during that verbal argument, this deputy was present and he heard everything. I forget that I was -- there were -- there were other people around. I mean there were somebody else with me." [Interpretation] So, did you also say in 2001 that the conversation was held from your office?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes, because I think that there was no phone anywhere else except at the office. That was where I talked to you from. I wondered somewhat and I had a heated discussion with you to a certain degree. I asked you what was going on and you told me something to the effect that, Those idiots used to do that, Vojo, without my knowledge. That was that, and it was a heated conversation. And it's true that I called you from the office because I never saw another telephone on that day. I could have called you from Prijedor as well also, but that wouldn't even have occurred to me; because I thought that they had done all this by your instructions, and then you said it had nothing to do with you and that those were the idiots who had done all that, to that effect. Perhaps you had in mind Stakic, or whether you had in mind the army. From this point in time I think that it was the army, but all right. The Muslims had attacked Prijedor. It wasn't the Serbs who launched the attack. Is there anything that I haven't said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. It's fine, thank you. I just wanted to ask you this, now that you said attacked, you listed a number of municipalities in which Muslims lived but had no problems: Are you aware of a municipality in Krajina in which the Patriotic League and the Green Berets did not begin the fighting and the Serbian army and police attacked and killed somebody?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No. They were -- I have the feeling that this part of the Muslim people were very impatient, so to speak. I think they -- they openly paraded with uniforms and weapons, and so on, in all municipalities, most often the municipalities where the Muslims were the relative majority or the Serb were the relative majority. I'm not aware of the Serbian army attacking first anywhere. In Kljuc and in Sanski Most, it was the Muslims who attacked first. In Prijedor, it was the Muslims who attacked first. Actually, we in Krajina didn't have any war. What happened in May and June, that was that. And after that there was no fighting, no conflicts or combat. Those who wanted to leave did so. I was in a room in Banja Luka somewhere close to the bridge, I got there on business and I saw a number of men and women, and I asked, What are these people doing here? And they told me, They are going abroad. What are they doing here? They said, They are getting some documents issued. And then I thought they are going abroad, well, that's not bad, better to go abroad than to be in the war. And why couldn't the Serbs from Sarajevo leave and go abroad? That was what I thought privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to rush and it will be interesting to read your experiences that have been written down. Today, you were asked as for the relations between Brdjanin and the leadership in Pale, and you were suggested that he was in close contact with the leadership, that he maintained such contacts. You said that he had a wish to maintain close contacts. And did you have any direct knowledge as to whether Brdjanin visited Pale in the leadership at the time and how frequently?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Very rarely. That's my opinion. He became a minister of town planning, if I'm not mistaken, and he was satisfied with that. I think he paid few visits and I know that on many occasions you attacked him because of his conduct and his irregularities. And very often it was asked, Why are you doing this, giving a goal to yourself, Brdjo? I didn't see or hear that but people reported it to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please add this page 3956 in Serbian and call up page 16 in English and 21 in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please slow down a little?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you both could slow down. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just remind the accused that the use of prior statements as we learned, perhaps at painful length today, is about -- arises in the impeachment process. So I think it's not unacceptable, of course, to use these things in redirect or direct, but they shouldn't be a first port of call for any aspects of the examination. But if Dr. Karadzic is proposing to go through various parts of the prior statement, he will have to -- I don't think that's a matter of leading and he'll have to ask questions that give rise to the appropriate method of doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the adding to -- adding of this page, page 39?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic. We will add that page, 39.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'm a bit confused. I just want to note that this document was used selectively by the OTP. Isn't it that it isn't as one may gain the impression. Here, from line 4 onwards, you were asked about that, whether you were aware of these visits, and you said that you really didn't know. Do you remember that you said so and do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: What? Under which number? Four, was it? Are you aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It has to do with Brdjanin. Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I don't know how frequently he went there but I don't think that you were on a close terms with Brdjanin. I don't think that he was somebody who had much in common with the political leadership, some other people did but not him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask for this page to be added and to be admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not a bit tenuous? He already confirmed that he rarely knows. But in any event, Mr. Tieger, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, on this one, I agree with the Court. I mean he asked him if he knew, he said he didn't. He asked him again if he didn't know, and then he pointed out -- it's reflected here. I -- you know, I -- I don't think that's an appropriate use of the document under these circumstances. I accept that there are uses to which it can be made in redirect, and I have no problem with that, but this doesn't seem like one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may give up on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we then proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, it was also suggested to you that the municipalities, without your maybe, had a direct contact with the president of the republic. Did the municipalities from Krajina during 1992 depend in their work on the leadership at Pale or were they independent from it? And what was the physical link up until the end of July or August, when the corridor was established?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: I think that there was no connection with Pale; that is to say the municipalities had no contacts with Pale. I stand by that. It was physically impossible for them to establish links with Pale because the territory was cut off in Posavina and we were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any direct knowledge of any example of municipal leaderships during the existence of the AR Krajina that it sent reports to or received instruction from the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to the relation of the president of municipalities, Mr. Karadzic. What did you mean by saying that by chain of command? You said there was a chain of command running from the municipalities to Karadzic. What did you mean by that chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in 1992, the year of war and war conflict, it was impossible physically to establish any sort of contact with the president of the republic or any other institutions at the republic level. We were surrounded, so how could it have been possible to do something like that? We were left to our own devices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was suggested to you today that the telephone lines were in operation, nevertheless. Can you tell us whether they worked all the time and was it always easy for us to communicate on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: No. They were not always functional. Sometimes they did, sometimes not. The power was down for months and the phone lines were down for months. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I ask you to go to some municipalities to do something? You did mention that and you spoke about that. Were you acting as a representative of the state, of the government, apart from the fact that you had your own goodwill, personally?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was doing that sort of work as if I was a kind of mini-statesman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the authorities were unable to help the Muslim and Croatian civilians, did you then address international organisations so that they would help the Muslim civilians who had set out?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN
utterances.text: Very frequently. For example, Mr. Schweizer was the president of the ICRC, and in all sorts of situations he would try to help us with regard to the Muslims and the Croats. With regard to the Croats, Caritas existed. It helped both to the Croats and the Serbs and the Muslims. And then there was a humanitarian association among the Muslims, what was it called, renewal or something like that, but they did not give a lot when Caritas did, and they had helped both the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show for a moment P3820. This has been admitted already. Can we please show the 6th of June, 1992. No, we need the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see this well, if you can please read it out or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I will read it out to you, and could we please show the English version. You are slightly promoted here. If you have a look, it says on the 1st of June, 1992, the mayor of Banja Luka, Mr. Kupresanin, called a civil affairs office in Sector North. He conveyed some information concerning the Muslim refugees' flow that might originate from his area towards Croatia, passing through the crossing points in Dvor and Karlovac, and so on. The mayor's information can be summarised as follows. And now you say that you are in contact with the presidents of municipalities in order to resolve the situation in which the Muslim population is, that this population is in fear, there is a shortage of food and medicine, that there is a lack of trust on part of the Muslim civilians with regard to the local authorities, that they had tried to go to Travnik which is under Croatian control, and so on. Do you remember and how often did you request from international humanitarian organisations to help you with your fellow citizens of a different religion?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please restart with his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, could you restart your answer? Could you repeat it from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said very often, especially the International Red Cross. In the case of Kotor Varos, there were two jeeps involved. We followed the column, the people, women, children. They always wanted to help is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I see the time. Excellencies, shall we continue tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kupresanin, we will adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. I'd like to advise you not to discuss --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you are giving testimony here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is one matter I'd like to adjourn -- I'd like to raise before we adjourn. It's related to the associated exhibits. The Chamber often -- as today, the Chamber often identifies the document being tendered as associated exhibits which are not indispensable and inseparable with the underlying statement, and invites the accused to lead these documents live, if he seeks to have them admitted, to provide more context. The accused -- the accused often decides not to seek to tender these documents, which suggests that those documents are not of such significance to the Defence case. The Chamber invites the accused, in consultation with Mr. Robinson and his team, to be more carefully -- in only tendering associated exhibits which form an indispensable and inseparable part of the witness's statement and which are of significance to his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we will do that, but I also would just like to indicate that we discussed this very point specifically after you have given us 25 hours of the 100 that we asked for in additional hours. And we decided for the remainder of this case we are going to give up on most of the associated exhibits that you don't admit, simply because we don't have enough time, even though we do think often that they are important. But we will try to do a better job of incorporating them into the statement, but you can expect in the future we will often not have enough time to lead live documents that are attempted to be associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be more vigilant and take more robust care in tendering the exhibits. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 15th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
